# Helper catalogue

Reusable capabilities of X-Kernel and its locked dependencies. Before writing a
helper, container, lock, parser or allocator, look for it here; the card
linked from each entry holds the evidence (file, item and quote) for every claim.
How the catalogue is kept current: [README.md](README.md).

> **Note:** Five cards need an owner decision and are not suggested until their open questions are answered: hash_digest_sha2, id_alloc_fd_slots_kfd, mm_user_load_vec_osvm, mm_user_range_check_kuaccess, parse_binary_zerocopy.

Contract values are quoted from the source; `unknown` means no evidence was
found, not that the property is absent. Check the card before relying on a
contract in IRQ, NMI or allocation-free code.

## Containers

### mpmc_queue_heapless

**Fixed-capacity MPMC queue (heapless::mpmc::Queue, deprecated constructor) - available but unused** — crates.io `heapless` 0.9.3; family `container.ring`; card [cards/mpmc_queue_heapless.yaml](cards/mpmc_queue_heapless.yaml)

heapless::mpmc::Queue&lt;T, N> is a fixed-capacity multiple-producer multiple-consumer queue. Its constructor is marked deprecated upstream because it is not truly lock-free: a preempted enqueue or dequeue can leave the queue in a state where other tasks cannot make progress, and enqueue/dequeue then return an error. No workspace crate uses it at the pin.

- Entry points: `heapless::mpmc::Queue`, `heapless::mpmc::Queue::new`
- Operations: `enqueue` (enqueue at the tail; Err(item) on full or a transient inability to progress caused by an interrupted operation); `dequeue` (dequeue at the head; None on empty or a transient inability to progress caused by an interrupted operation)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (heapless is #![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)]; the mpmc module needs atomics, see notes)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the queue owns the items; a rejected enqueue hands the item back
  - errors / bounds: fixed capacity; enqueue/dequeue can also fail if another task was preempted mid-operation
  - concurrency: MPMC, but not truly lock-free - a preempted operation can block progress of others (documented as deprecated)
- Usage:
  1. Use Queue::new only after accepting the upstream deprecation and progress limitation; it is not a lock-free object pool. N must satisfy the constructor checks. enqueue Err(item) and dequeue None can mean transient failure after a preempted operation, so neither proves full/empty in all schedules.
- Do not use it when:
  - upstream marks the constructor deprecated: not truly lock-free, unsuitable as an object pool
  - needs target atomics (cfg on target_has_atomic); for one producer and one consumer prefer spsc_ring_ringbuf

### spsc_ring_ringbuf

**Lock-free SPSC FIFO ring buffer with producer/consumer split (ringbuf::HeapRb / StaticRb)** — crates.io `ringbuf` 0.4.8; family `container.ring`; card [cards/spsc_ring_ringbuf.yaml](cards/spsc_ring_ringbuf.yaml)

Single-producer single-consumer FIFO ring buffer from the ringbuf crate. SharedRb can be split into a Producer and a Consumer handle used from different threads or CPUs; HeapRb stores items on the heap, StaticRb in inline storage with const capacity; LocalRb is the non-synchronised single-thread variant.

- Entry points: `ringbuf::HeapRb`, `ringbuf::StaticRb`, `ringbuf::SharedRb`, `ringbuf::LocalRb`
- Operations: `split` (turn the ring buffer into a (producer, consumer) pair); `try_push` (append one item; on a full buffer the item is handed back in Err); `try_pop` (remove the eldest item; None when empty); `push_overwrite` (on the unsplit buffer, overwrite the oldest item when full (the overwritten item is returned))
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (crate is #![no_std]; HeapRb needs the alloc feature)
  - allocation: HeapRb allocates its storage once at construction; StaticRb stores contents inline without heap; push/pop do not allocate (storage is fixed-capacity)
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the buffer owns the items; try_push gives the item back on a full buffer; HeapProd/HeapCons share the ring through an Arc
  - errors / bounds: capacity is fixed (NonZeroUsize); try_push returns Err(item) when full and try_pop returns None when empty; StaticRb capacity must be non-zero
  - concurrency: SharedRb is lock-free SPSC (one producer and one consumer); LocalRb is for single-threaded use only
- Usage:
  1. create HeapRb::new(capacity) or StaticRb::default(), then rb.split() into producer and consumer halves
- Do not use it when:
  - single producer and single consumer only; not an MPMC or multi-producer queue (the crate has no MPMC type)
  - fixed capacity; does not grow
  - the crate gives no statement on IRQ/NMI use; do not suggest it for interrupt-context producers without checking
  - not a replacement for a device-defined descriptor ring such as a virtio virtqueue

### fixed_vec_arrayvec

**Fixed-capacity array-backed vector and string (arrayvec::ArrayVec / ArrayString)** — crates.io `arrayvec` 0.7.8; family `container.fixed_capacity`; card [cards/fixed_vec_arrayvec.yaml](cards/fixed_vec_arrayvec.yaml)

ArrayVec&lt;T, CAP> is a Vec-like container that stores its contents inline in an array and never allocates; push panics when full, try_push returns CapacityError. ArrayString is the string equivalent.

- Entry points: `arrayvec::ArrayVec`, `arrayvec::ArrayVec::new`, `arrayvec::ArrayVec::new_const`
- Operations: `push` (append; panics if the vector is full); `try_push` (append; returns CapacityError carrying the element if full); `construct` (empty vector, capacity fixed by the CAP generic; new_const is a const fn for statics)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes when the std feature is disabled (#![cfg_attr(not(feature="std"), no_std)]; std is a default feature)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: stores elements inline in the value itself; a failed try_push returns the element in CapacityError
  - errors / bounds: capacity is the const generic CAP; push panics when full; try_push / try_insert / try_extend_from_slice return CapacityError
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. ArrayVec::&lt;T, CAP>::new() then prefer try_push where overflow is possible
- Do not use it when:
  - never grows; if the element count is unbounded use alloc Vec or smallvec (inline_vec_smallvec)
  - push panics when full - use try_push in code paths that must not panic
  - heapless::Vec (fixed_vec_heapless) is the near-equivalent whose push returns Err instead of panicking

### fixed_vec_heapless

**Fixed-capacity inline vector without heap (heapless::Vec)** — crates.io `heapless` 0.9.3; family `container.fixed_capacity`; card [cards/fixed_vec_heapless.yaml](cards/fixed_vec_heapless.yaml)

heapless::Vec&lt;T, N> is a Vec-like container with compile-time capacity N stored inline (stack, static or struct field). push returns the item back when full; nothing is ever allocated. An optional length type (e.g. u16) shrinks the length field.

- Entry points: `heapless::Vec`, `heapless::Vec::new`
- Operations: `construct` (const constructor, empty vector with capacity N (usable in a static)); `push` (append; returns the item back (Err(item)) if the vector is full); `extend_from_slice` (append a slice; Err(CapacityError) when it does not fit)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)])
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the vector owns its elements inline; a rejected push hands the item back
  - errors / bounds: capacity fixed at compile time; push returns Err(item), extend_from_slice returns Err(CapacityError) when full
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. pick a capacity N at compile time; use the LenT parameter (e.g. u16) only when the default usize length is too large
- Do not use it when:
  - capacity is fixed at compile time; if the element count is unbounded use alloc::vec::Vec
  - for a fixed vector with spill-to-heap use smallvec (card inline_vec_smallvec); for the arrayvec flavour see fixed_vec_arrayvec

### inline_vec_smallvec

**Vector with inline storage that spills to the heap (smallvec::SmallVec)** — crates.io `smallvec` 1.16.3; family `container.inline_vec`; card [cards/inline_vec_smallvec.yaml](cards/inline_vec_smallvec.yaml)

SmallVec&lt;[T; N]> stores up to N elements inline and moves to a heap allocation only when it grows past N. Useful for lists that are almost always short (poll registrations, resource descriptors, small handle sets) where a Vec allocation per instance is wasteful.

- Entry points: `smallvec::SmallVec`, `smallvec::SmallVec::new`, `smallvec::SmallVec::new_const`
- Operations: `construct` (empty vector; new_const is the const fn variant (needs the const_new feature, arrays only)); `push` (append; may spill to the heap); `spilled` (whether the data now lives in a heap buffer); `try_reserve` (fallible growth; returns CollectionAllocErr instead of aborting)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std]; the optional write feature depends on std)
  - allocation: new() starts with inline storage; growth beyond inline capacity may spill to a heap buffer. Explicit reserve/with_capacity may allocate even with length &lt;= inline capacity; try_reserve is fallible.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: owns its elements, inline or in its heap buffer
  - errors / bounds: growth through push/insert panics on capacity overflow; the try_reserve family returns CollectionAllocErr
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. choose an inline capacity N with type SmallVec&lt;[T; N]>; elements beyond N cause a heap allocation
- Do not use it when:
  - allocates once it exceeds the inline capacity; do not use where heap allocation is forbidden - use fixed_vec_arrayvec or fixed_vec_heapless instead
  - workspace root enables features const_generics, const_new and union; crates with their own dependency line may enable different features

### fixed_bitmap_bitmaps

**Fixed-size const-generic bitmap with set/get/first-index search (bitmaps::Bitmap)** — crates.io `bitmaps` 3.2.1; family `container.bitmap`; card [cards/fixed_bitmap_bitmaps.yaml](cards/fixed_bitmap_bitmaps.yaml)

Bitmap&lt;SIZE> is a compact bit set of compile-time size (up to 1024 bits) stored in the smallest integer or u128 array that fits. It offers get/set (returns the previous value), count, first/next true index, first false index and invert. Suitable for key-state tables, event-type masks and "slot occupied" maps; first_false_index gives a lowest-free-slot search.

- Entry points: `bitmaps::Bitmap`, `bitmaps::Bitmap::new`
- Operations: `set` (set or clear one bit; returns the previous value); `first_free` (index of the lowest clear bit, or None when all bits are set); `next_set` (iterate over set bits); `count` (number of true bits)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes when the std feature is off (#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]; std is a default feature)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: plain value type holding the bits inline (integer or u128 array); the query methods take self by value
  - errors / bounds: size is a const generic, at most 1024 bits; get/set check index &lt; SIZE only with debug_assert (no check in release builds)
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. Bitmap::&lt;N>::new() then set(i, true) / get(i); indices must be below SIZE
- Do not use it when:
  - compile-time size, maximum 1024 bits; a bitmap sized at runtime needs another structure
  - no atomic operations - concurrent updates need an external lock or atomics
  - this is a bit set, not a typed flag set: for named flag constants use flags_bitflags

### intrusive_list_intrusive_collections

**Intrusive doubly-linked list with caller-owned nodes (intrusive_collections::LinkedList)** — crates.io `intrusive-collections` 0.10.2; family `container.list`; card [cards/intrusive_list_intrusive_collections.yaml](cards/intrusive_list_intrusive_collections.yaml)

LinkedList&lt;A> links objects through an embedded Link / AtomicLink field and never allocates for list nodes; an Adapter (usually generated with intrusive_adapter!) says how to reach the link and which pointer type (Box, Arc, UnsafeRef, ...) owns the element. O(1) push/pop at both ends and O(1) removal through a cursor. AtomicLink makes the link shareable between threads. Used for work queues, wait lists, RCU callback queues and allocator free lists.

- Entry points: `intrusive_collections::LinkedList`, `intrusive_collections::LinkedList::new`
- Operations: `push_back` (link an owned pointer into the list at an end; no allocation); `pop` (unlink and return the owned pointer of an end element); `cursor_remove` (positioned insert_before / insert_after / remove through a CursorMut)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: the list itself never allocates for nodes (links live in the elements)
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: ownership follows the Adapter pointer type; dropping the list converts all linked elements back to owned pointers and drops them; UnsafeRef leaves freeing to the user
  - errors / bounds: `unknown`
  - concurrency: no internal locking; the Link type is not thread-shareable but AtomicLink is "shared between threads" - callers still need external synchronisation for list mutation
- Usage:
  1. embed a LinkedListLink (or LinkedListAtomicLink for cross-thread use) in the element, declare an adapter with intrusive_adapter!, then LinkedList::new(Adapter::NEW or new())
- Do not use it when:
  - pointer-ownership and link lifetime rules are unsafe-adjacent: an element must outlive its membership unless the pointer type is owning (Box/Arc)
  - no internal synchronisation; wrap in a lock when shared
  - an element can be in only one list per link field; add a second link field for a second list
  - linked_list_r4l (card intrusive_list_r4l) is the other intrusive list in the tree, with a different Links/GetLinks API

### intrusive_list_r4l

**Intrusive list with O(1) arbitrary removal over Box/Arc elements (linked_list_r4l::List)** — crates.io `linked_list_r4l` 0.3.0; family `container.list`; card [cards/intrusive_list_r4l.yaml](cards/intrusive_list_r4l.yaml)

linked_list_r4l::List&lt;G> is an intrusive doubly-linked list ported from Rust-for-Linux. Elements embed a Links&lt;T> field, expose it through the GetLinks trait, and are wrapped in Box or Arc; the list takes ownership while linked. Offers push_back / push_front / pop_front, unsafe remove of a given entry and cursors. Links tracks membership with an atomic flag so double insertion is rejected.

- Entry points: `linked_list_r4l::List`, `linked_list_r4l::List::new`
- Operations: `push_back` (link a wrapped (Box/Arc) element at the tail); `pop_front` (unlink and return the head element; None when empty); `remove` (unsafe removal of a specific element in constant time)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)])
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the list owns wrapped (Box/Arc) elements while they are linked; remove is unsafe and requires the entry to be on this list or in none
  - errors / bounds: `unknown`
  - concurrency: Links is Send/Sync when the entry is; no locking is provided for list mutation (needs external synchronisation)
- Usage:
  1. embed Links&lt;Self> in the element (Links::new()), implement GetLinks::get_links for the wrapper type, then use List&lt;Box&lt;T>> / List&lt;Arc&lt;T>>
- Do not use it when:
  - a second intrusive list implementation exists (card intrusive_list_intrusive_collections) with adapters, cursors and RBTree siblings; prefer whichever the surrounding crate already uses
  - no internal locking

### intrusive_rbtree_intrusive_collections

**Intrusive red-black tree ordered by key (intrusive_collections::RBTree)** — crates.io `intrusive-collections` 0.10.2; family `container.tree`; card [cards/intrusive_rbtree_intrusive_collections.yaml](cards/intrusive_rbtree_intrusive_collections.yaml)

RBTree&lt;A> keeps objects ordered by a key through an embedded RBTreeLink / RBTreeAtomicLink; a KeyAdapter provides the key. Supports find, lower_bound / upper_bound, range, ordered cursors and O(log n) insert and remove without allocating tree nodes. Used for timer deadlines, scheduler run queues and a pty-pair index.

- Entry points: `intrusive_collections::RBTree`, `intrusive_collections::RBTree::new`
- Operations: `insert` (insert an owned pointer in key order); `find` (cursor at the element with the given key); `lower_bound` (first element at or after a bound (ordered successor query))
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: the tree itself never allocates for nodes (links live in the elements)
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: dropping the tree converts linked elements back to owned pointers and drops them; the ordering invariant is the caller's responsibility (memory-safe if violated, results may be wrong)
  - errors / bounds: `unknown`
  - concurrency: no internal locking; AtomicLink only makes the link type shareable between threads
- Usage:
  1. embed an RBTreeLink (or RBTreeAtomicLink), declare the adapter, and implement KeyAdapter for the key; keep keys unchanged while linked
- Do not use it when:
  - keys must not change while the element is linked; the tree does not detect violations
  - ordered map with owned nodes and allocation is alloc::collections::BTreeMap, not this crate
  - not an integer-indexed lookup table: for sparse usize keys see sparse_index_xarray

### sparse_index_xarray

**RCU-readable sparse usize-indexed owning index (kxarray::XArray)** — crate `kxarray` (`util/kxarray`); family `container.sparse_index`; card [cards/sparse_index_xarray.yaml](cards/sparse_index_xarray.yaml)

Radix-style sparse map from usize keys to owned Box/Arc values. Readers borrow entries inside an RCU read scope without locks or allocation; writers serialise on an internal spin lock and retire displaced owners through RCU callbacks.

- Entry points: [`kxarray::XArray`](../../util/kxarray/src/lib.rs), [`kxarray::XArray::new`](../../util/kxarray/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `construct` (empty index, no allocation); `lookup` (read borrows without incrementing a count; get_owned exists for XArray&lt;Arc&lt;T>> and increments a strong count so the returned Arc may outlive both scope and array); `insert_if_absent` (insert only when the key is free; returns the value back on conflict); `replace` (insert or replace; the old owner is retired after a grace period); `remove` (remove an association; returns whether one was removed)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: allocates on insert / set (infallible kernel OOM policy); read does not allocate
  - blocking: read scopes must not sleep; set / remove need a sleepable, watched task context
  - IRQ / NMI: writers never from IRQ, softirq or NMI; Drop not from NMI
  - ownership: the array owns each inserted Box, or one strong count of each Arc; ownership moves only on success
  - errors / bounds: insert returns Err(value) when occupied; set / remove return the RCU preflight KError
  - concurrency: lock-free RCU readers; writers serialised by an internal SpinNoPreempt
- Usage:
  1. construct with XArray::new (const, no allocation)
  2. insert / set / remove from a task context, inside `unsafe` with the adoption contract audited
  3. read inside krcu::with_read; the borrow cannot escape the scope
- Do not use it when:
  - not an ID allocator — callers choose the key; there is no find-free-index operation
  - stored data needs its own mutation protocol; the index only manages ownership of the slot
  - not for IRQ / NMI writers

### map_hashbrown

**no_std hash map and set (hashbrown::HashMap / HashSet)** — crates.io `hashbrown` 0.16.1; family `container.map`; card [cards/map_hashbrown.yaml](cards/map_hashbrown.yaml)

hashbrown is the SwissTable port that backs std's HashMap. HashMap&lt;K, V> and HashSet&lt;T> work without std, hash with foldhash by default, and offer entry(), try_reserve (fallible growth) and an allocator type parameter. It is the kernel's general unordered key-to-value map.

- Entry points: `hashbrown::HashMap`, `hashbrown::HashSet`, `hashbrown::HashMap::with_capacity`, `hashbrown::HashMap::with_hasher`
- Operations: `insert` (insert or replace; returns the previous value); `lookup` (lookup by Q: Hash + Equivalent&lt;K> + ?Sized; borrowed forms work when their equality/hash agree with the stored key); `remove` (remove by key and return the value); `entry` (single-lookup get-or-insert API); `try_reserve` (reserve space and report allocation failure as TryReserveError instead of aborting)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes: #![no_std]; the kernel's workspace dependency leaves default features on (default-hasher = foldhash, allocator-api2, ...), none of which is std
  - allocation: heap allocated through an Allocator parameter that defaults to Global; try_reserve exposes allocation failure
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the map owns keys and values; unordered
  - errors / bounds: lookups return Option; try_reserve returns TryReserveError; growth through insert uses the allocator's failure path
  - concurrency: mutating operations take &mut self
- Usage:
  1. keys must not be attacker-chosen when the default hasher is used; pass a keyed hasher through with_hasher if untrusted input decides the keys
- Do not use it when:
  - iteration order is unspecified; for ordered keys use an ordered map from alloc (BTreeMap)
  - the default hasher does not defend against HashDoS; do not key it on unauthenticated input without a keyed hasher
  - kvfs pins hashbrown 0.15 (a second lock entry); this card is the 0.16 line used by the other crates
  - for a table keyed by small integer ids prefer slot_pool_slab or sparse_index_xarray

### map_weak_map

**Ordered map holding weak references that expire silently (weak_map::WeakMap)** — crates.io `weak-map` 0.1.2; family `container.map`; card [cards/map_weak_map.yaml](cards/map_weak_map.yaml)

WeakMap&lt;K, V> wraps a BTreeMap whose values are Weak/Rc-Weak handles. insert takes a strong reference and stores a downgraded one; get upgrades on lookup and returns None for an expired entry; expired entries are swept by cleanup(), which runs automatically after enough operations. The kernel uses it for the session-to-process-group registry where the map must not keep objects alive.

- Entry points: `weak_map::WeakMap`, `weak_map::WeakMap::new`
- Operations: `insert` (store a downgraded handle under the key; returns the previous value if it is still alive); `get` (look up and upgrade; None when the key is missing or the value has expired); `cleanup` (drop all expired entries; also triggered automatically when the operation counter reaches a threshold); `len` (len counts only live entries and is linear; raw_len includes expired ones; new does not allocate)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes: #![no_std] (stores Rc/Arc handles from alloc)
  - allocation: new() does not allocate; entries are BTreeMap nodes
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the map never keeps a value alive; entries whose strong owners are gone read as absent and are removed lazily
  - errors / bounds: lookups return Option; the key type must be Ord; len() and cleanup() are linear in the number of entries
  - concurrency: mutating operations take &mut self; kprocess wraps it in SpinNoIrq
- Do not use it when:
  - ordered by key (BTreeMap): lookups are O(log n); for hashing keys use map_hashbrown with Weak values yourself
  - len() and cleanup() are linear; do not call them on a hot path with a large map
  - expiry is only noticed lazily; entries are removed at cleanup, so memory held by dead keys lingers until then

### slot_pool_slab

**Slot pool that hands out reusable usize keys (slab::Slab)** — crates.io `slab` 0.4.12; family `container.slot_pool`; card [cards/slot_pool_slab.yaml](cards/slot_pool_slab.yaml)

Slab&lt;T> is a Vec-backed pre-allocated store: insert(value) picks a vacant slot and returns its usize key, get/get_mut/remove take that key, and freed keys are reused by later inserts. vacant_entry gives the key before the value is built. It is the crate used for handle tables and id-to-object stores in the filesystem and TEE crates.

- Entry points: `slab::Slab`, `slab::Slab::new`, `slab::Slab::with_capacity`
- Operations: `insert` (store a value in a vacant slot and return its usize key); `vacant_entry` (reserve a slot and learn its key before the value is constructed); `lookup` (Option access by key; None for a vacant or out-of-range key); `remove` (take the value out and free the key for reuse; try_remove returns Option, remove panics on an invalid key)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes: #![no_std] unconditionally (std feature only adds extern crate std); the workspace dependency sets default-features = false
  - allocation: heap allocated; entries live in a Vec that grows on insert (with_capacity and reserve pre-size it)
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the slab owns the stored values; keys are plain usize and are reused after removal
  - errors / bounds: get/get_mut/try_remove return None for a vacant or out-of-range key; remove panics with "invalid key"
  - concurrency: mutating operations take &mut self; no internal locking is visible in the API
- Usage:
  1. insert returns the key; keep it as the handle. A removed key may be handed out again, so drop every copy of a handle when removing and prefer try_remove where the key is not trusted
- Do not use it when:
  - keys are not generation-checked: a stale key can name a different value after reuse; do not use it where use-after-free handles must be detected
  - the key is chosen by the slab; for caller-chosen sparse integer keys use sparse_index_xarray
  - unrelated to the kernel slab object allocator (mm.slab); this crate is a keyed container, not a memory allocator
  - the kalloc / alloc-engine feature named slab selects the in-tree slab allocator engine, not this crate

## ID allocation

### id_alloc_fd_slots_kfd

**Lowest-free-id slot table with occupancy bitmap (kfd FileSlots, crate-private)** — crate `kfd` (`process/kfd`); family `id.allocator`; card [cards/id_alloc_fd_slots_kfd.yaml](cards/id_alloc_fd_slots_kfd.yaml)

> **Needs an owner decision.** Do not suggest it until these are answered:
> - `symbols`: FileSlots is pub(crate) and fd_slots is private to kfd. Should kfd extract or publish an ID-slot interface for other crates, or should suggestions stay limited to kfd?

An internal find-lowest-free-index table. FileSlots&lt;T> stores up to FILE_LIMIT values in numbered slots with a u64-word occupancy bitmap and a free-slot lower bound; add / alloc(minimum, end) assign the lowest free id (O(words), skipping full words), add_at claims a fixed id, remove frees it. It is pub(crate) inside kfd and sized by krlimit::FILE_LIMIT, so it is a pattern to reuse or extract, not a dependency other crates can take today.

- Entry points: [`kfd::fd_slots::FileSlots`](../../process/kfd/src/fd_slots.rs), [`kfd::fd_slots::FileSlots::new`](../../process/kfd/src/fd_slots.rs)
- Operations: `alloc` (assigns the value the lowest free id in [minimum, end) and returns it; returns the value back in Err when no id is free); `remove` (frees the id, lowers the free bound, returns the stored value)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (kfd is #![no_std])
  - allocation: the table stores its fixed-capacity slots and occupancy bitmap inline; this does not constrain allocation by T or its destructor. It is not a public standalone pool.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the table owns stored values; a set bit means the slot holds an initialized value; Drop drops the live values; remove moves the value out
  - errors / bounds: fixed capacity krlimit::FILE_LIMIT; add / alloc / add_at return Err(value) when full, out of range or the id is taken; the exclusive end is clipped to CAPACITY
  - concurrency: no internal synchronization (&mut self for mutation); the caller serializes access (the fd table wraps it)
- Do not use it when:
  - pub(crate) inside kfd and sized by krlimit::FILE_LIMIT (1024): not a general ID allocator; other crates cannot depend on it without extracting it
  - it stores values and always returns the LOWEST free id (POSIX fd semantics); for monotonically increasing never-reused ids use counters (pid, timer ids)
  - no internal locking; no blocking when full
  - Visibility is pub(crate) and the fd_slots module is private. Treat as an internal pattern only: suppress replacement suggestions outside kfd until the owner approves extraction or a public API.

## Locks, waiting and synchronisation

### spin_lock_noirq

**IRQ-disabling, preemption-disabling spin lock (kspin::SpinNoIrq)** — crate `kspin` (`task/kspin`); family `sync.spinlock`; card [cards/spin_lock_noirq.yaml](cards/spin_lock_noirq.yaml)

Spin lock whose lock() first disables preemption and saves/disables local IRQs, then spins on an atomic flag (smp feature); dropping the guard releases the flag and restores IRQ and preemption state. Documented as usable from interrupt handlers. Never sleeps; critical sections must not block.

- Entry points: [`kspin::SpinNoIrq`](../../task/kspin/src/lib.rs), [`kspin::SpinLock::new`](../../task/kspin/src/lock.rs)
- Operations: `lock` (acquires guard state (preempt off, IRQs saved and disabled) then spins until the flag is taken); `try_lock` (single compare-exchange attempt; on failure the guard state is released and None is returned)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: spins, never sleeps; lock() on an already-held lock may panic or deadlock (not re-entrant)
  - IRQ / NMI: documented as the option usable from interrupt handlers (IRQs disabled while held); NMI usage is not stated
  - ownership: lock owns the protected value; RAII guard derefs to it and releases on drop; ordering is preempt-off first, IRQ restore first on release
  - errors / bounds: try_lock returns Option; no error type
  - concurrency: atomic flag only with the smp feature; without it the lock state is optimized away (single core)
- Usage:
  1. declare `static X: SpinNoIrq<T> = SpinNoIrq::new(v)` (const constructor) and use `X.lock()` for a short critical section
  2. guard drop releases the lock and restores IRQ and preemption state
- Do not use it when:
  - never use in sleepable code paths that need to block while holding it; use ksync::Mutex or ksync::RwLock for critical sections that sleep
  - SpinNoPreempt leaves IRQs enabled and SpinRaw does neither; they are not substitutes when an IRQ handler touches the same data (see spin_lock_nopreempt, spin_lock_raw)
  - reader-writer variant is a separate card: spin_rwlock_noirq
  - NoPreempt guard behavior depends on the preempt feature and host/kernel cfg. IRQ masking does not exclude NMI; do not use as a blanket NMI-safe lock or replace a lock-free NMI protocol.

### spin_lock_nopreempt

**Preemption-disabling spin lock that leaves IRQs enabled (kspin::SpinNoPreempt)** — crate `kspin` (`task/kspin`); family `sync.spinlock`; card [cards/spin_lock_nopreempt.yaml](cards/spin_lock_nopreempt.yaml)

Spin lock whose guard disables kernel preemption (via TaskPreemptionIf, only with the `preempt` feature) but does not touch IRQ state. Suitable when no IRQ handler accesses the same data or the caller already runs with IRQs disabled.

- Entry points: [`kspin::SpinNoPreempt`](../../task/kspin/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `lock` (disables preemption, then spins on the atomic flag when smp is enabled)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: spins; lock() may panic or deadlock if already held by the caller
  - IRQ / NMI: does not disable IRQs, so unsafe for data also used by IRQ handlers on the same CPU; NMI not stated
  - ownership: lock owns the value; RAII guard releases on drop and re-enables preemption
  - errors / bounds: try_lock returns Option; no error type
  - concurrency: atomic flag only with the smp feature; preemption control only with the preempt feature
- Usage:
  1. use only for data that no IRQ handler touches (or when IRQs are already disabled)
- Do not use it when:
  - not for data shared with IRQ handlers; use spin_lock_noirq (kspin::SpinNoIrq) instead
  - not a sleeping lock; use ksync::Mutex for critical sections that block

### spin_lock_raw

**Guard-less spin lock for contexts that already disabled IRQs and preemption (kspin::SpinRaw)** — crate `kspin` (`task/kspin`); family `sync.spinlock`; card [cards/spin_lock_raw.yaml](cards/spin_lock_raw.yaml)

SpinLock with the NoOp guard: lock() only spins on the flag and does not disable preemption or IRQs. Documented as a lock that must only be used where preemption and IRQs are already disabled.

- Entry points: [`kspin::SpinRaw`](../../task/kspin/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `lock` (spins on the atomic flag with no context protection)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: spins; may panic or deadlock if already held by the caller
  - IRQ / NMI: provides no IRQ protection; documented warning that IRQs and preemption must already be disabled
  - ownership: lock owns the value; RAII guard releases the flag on drop
  - errors / bounds: try_lock returns Option; no error type
  - concurrency: atomic flag only with the smp feature
- Usage:
  1. enter only from code that already holds IRQs and preemption off (for example inside another SpinNoIrq section)
- Do not use it when:
  - Use only when the documented IRQ/preemption exclusion already holds. A NoOp guard alone provides no NMI safety: an NMI can still deadlock if it interrupts a holder of the same lock.

### blocking_mutex

**Sleeping task mutex with adaptive spinning (kmutex::Mutex, re-exported as ksync::Mutex)** — crate `kmutex` (`sync/kmutex`); family `sync.mutex`; card [cards/blocking_mutex.yaml](cards/blocking_mutex.yaml)

lock_api-based mutex that records the owning task key, spins adaptively, then registers an event-listener and sleeps through TaskExecutionIf::block_on until unlock wakes one waiter. Requires sleepable task context; recursion panics; guards cannot move to another task.

- Entry points: [`kmutex::Mutex`](../../sync/kmutex/src/mutex.rs), [`kmutex::Mutex::new`](../../sync/kmutex/src/mutex.rs)
- Operations: `lock` (CAS the owner key; adaptive spin; register listener, recheck owner, then sleep until woken); `unlock` (clears the owner key (asserting the caller is the owner) and wakes one listener)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: sleeps after bounded adaptive spinning; requires sleepable task context; recursion panics
  - IRQ / NMI: not usable from IRQ or softirq (requires sleepable task context); NMI not stated
  - ownership: guard is not Send; the owning task may migrate CPUs while holding it; owner key stays valid across blocking and migration
  - errors / bounds: lock() has no error return; recursive acquisition panics
  - concurrency: atomic owner id; unlock wakes one listener; no starvation-freedom promise stated here
- Usage:
  1. Use the public wrapper and .lock() or .read()/.write() only in sleepable task context. For static initialization use ksync::static_lock! when stats is enabled; new() is const only without stats.
  2. the linked task runtime must provide kiface_task_api::TaskExecutionIf (identity, yield, wait)
- Do not use it when:
  - Blocking acquisition requires sleepable task context. Select a spinlock only after checking its IRQ, preemption and NMI contract; SpinNoIrq is not a general NMI-safe replacement.
  - does not by itself provide reader-writer sharing (use ksync::RwLock) or counting (use ksync::Semaphore)

### mutex_wrapper_lock_api

**Generic Mutex / RwLock / guard types over a user-supplied raw lock (lock_api)** — crates.io `lock_api` 0.4.14; family `sync.mutex`; card [cards/mutex_wrapper_lock_api.yaml](cards/mutex_wrapper_lock_api.yaml)

lock_api supplies the data-owning Mutex&lt;R, T>, RwLock&lt;R, T> and RAII guards; the caller implements only the raw protocol (RawMutex::lock / try_lock / unlock, RawRwLock) and a GuardMarker (GuardSend or GuardNoSend). The kernel's blocking Mutex and RwLock are lock_api wrappers over an in-tree raw lock, and ktracing builds its tracing lock the same way. Use it when a new lock flavour needs the standard guard API without re-writing guards and data cells.

- Entry points: `lock_api::RawMutex`, `lock_api::Mutex`, `lock_api::Mutex::const_new`, `lock_api::RawRwLock`, `lock_api::RwLock`, `lock_api::RwLock::const_new`
- Operations: `implement_raw_lock` (provide INIT, GuardMarker, lock, try_lock and unsafe unlock; implementations must really be exclusive); `wrap` (build a data-owning lock from a raw lock value in const context); `lock` (try_lock returns Option&lt;guard>; recursive lock is unsupported and depends on the raw implementation (it may deadlock or panic, as kmutex does); there is no standardized recursive-lock error)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes: #![no_std]; the workspace dependency sets default-features = false (alloc is touched only by the arc_lock feature)
  - allocation: the lock and guard types hold the data inline; the alloc crate is used only with the arc_lock feature
  - blocking: whether lock blocks, spins or disables interrupts is decided by the RawMutex implementation; the trait documents lock as blocking the current thread
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the lock owns the data in an UnsafeCell and hands out RAII guards; GuardMarker selects whether a guard is Send
  - errors / bounds: try_lock returns Option&lt;guard>; recursive lock is unsupported and depends on the raw implementation (it may deadlock or panic, as kmutex does); there is no standardized recursive-lock error
  - concurrency: RawMutex is an unsafe trait whose implementations must guarantee exclusion; unlock may only be paired with a held lock
- Usage:
  1. implement RawMutex (or RawRwLock) for the lock state, choose GuardSend or GuardNoSend, then expose lock_api::Mutex&lt;YourRaw, T> through a thin newtype or alias (as kmutex does) so call sites keep using guards
- Do not use it when:
  - this is a wrapper crate, not a lock algorithm: it provides no waiting policy; wait/wake or spinning must come from the RawMutex implementation (see blocking_mutex and the spin_lock_* cards)
  - the kernel's spinlocks (kspin) have their own guard types and do not go through lock_api, so do not wrap SpinNoIrq in lock_api::Mutex to get an IRQ-disabling lock
  - ReentrantMutex support exists in lock_api but needs a thread-id provider; kernel tasks do not currently use it

### blocking_rwlock

**Sleeping reader-writer lock with optimistic spinning (ksync::RwLock)** — crate `ksync` (`task/ksync`); family `sync.rwlock`; card [cards/blocking_rwlock.yaml](cards/blocking_rwlock.yaml)

lock_api RwLock over an atomic state word (high bit write-locked, low 31 bits reader count) with separate reader and writer event-listeners. Contended acquires spin, then sleep via ktask::future::block_on. The recorded writer is tracked for spinners; readers are not recorded.

- Entry points: [`ksync::RwLock`](../../task/ksync/src/rwlock.rs), [`ksync::RwLock::new`](../../task/ksync/src/rwlock.rs)
- Operations: `read` (shared acquire; registers a reader listener, rechecks the write bit, then blocks); `write` (exclusive acquire; registers a writer listener then blocks)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: sleeps (event-listener + ktask block_on) after bounded spinning; acquiring while this task is the recorded writer panics
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: lock owns the value through lock_api guards; guard marker is GuardSend
  - errors / bounds: panics when the reader count would reach MAX_READERS (2^31 - 1)
  - concurrency: waiting does not reserve the lock; no starvation-freedom promise
- Usage:
  1. Use the public wrapper and .lock() or .read()/.write() only in sleepable task context. For static initialization use ksync::static_lock! when stats is enabled; new() is const only without stats.
- Do not use it when:
  - not for IRQ or other non-sleeping contexts; use kspin::SpinRwNoIrq there (spin_rwlock_noirq)
  - no lock-upgrade or downgrade operations are documented in this crate

### spin_rwlock_noirq

**IRQ-disabling reader-writer spin lock (kspin::SpinRwNoIrq)** — crate `kspin` (`task/kspin`); family `sync.rwlock`; card [cards/spin_rwlock_noirq.yaml](cards/spin_rwlock_noirq.yaml)

Reader-writer spin lock whose read and write guards both disable preemption and IRQs. Allows concurrent readers or one writer in short, non-sleeping critical sections.

- Entry points: [`kspin::SpinRwNoIrq`](../../task/kspin/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `read` (acquire guard state, then spin while a writer holds the lock, then increment the reader count); `write` (exclusive spinning acquisition)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: spins; cannot sleep
  - IRQ / NMI: both reader and writer disable preemption and IRQs; IRQ-visible sections are the stated use; NMI not stated
  - ownership: lock owns the value; RAII read/write guards release on drop
  - errors / bounds: try_read / try_write return Option; read panics on reader-count overflow (2^63 - 1 readers)
  - concurrency: many readers or one writer; readers spin while a writer holds the lock; no fairness statement
- Usage:
  1. use for short, non-sleeping shared/exclusive sections that IRQ handlers may also enter
- Do not use it when:
  - no sleeping; for blocking readers/writers use ksync::RwLock (blocking_rwlock)
  - only the NoPreemptIrqSave instantiation has an alias; other guard types are possible through SpinRwLock&lt;G, T> but are not documented
  - NoPreempt guard behavior depends on the preempt feature and host/kernel cfg. IRQ masking does not exclude NMI; do not use as a blanket NMI-safe lock or replace a lock-free NMI protocol.

### counting_semaphore

**Blocking counting semaphore (ksync::Semaphore)** — crate `ksync` (`task/ksync`); family `sync.semaphore`; card [cards/counting_semaphore.yaml](cards/counting_semaphore.yaml)

Atomic permit counter plus an event-listener. acquire() CAS-decrements the count, or registers a listener, rechecks the count, and blocks with ktask::future::block_on. release() increments and wakes one additional waiter. SemaphoreGuard releases on drop.

- Entry points: [`ksync::Semaphore`](../../task/ksync/src/semaphore.rs), [`ksync::Semaphore::new`](../../task/ksync/src/semaphore.rs)
- Operations: `acquire` (blocks until a permit is available; listener registered before the final count recheck); `release` (adds a permit and wakes one previously unnotified waiter)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: acquire blocks the calling task (event-listener + ktask::future::block_on)
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: SemaphoreGuard releases its permit on drop; release() does not cap the count at the initial permits
  - errors / bounds: try_acquire returns bool after a bounded retry loop (10 CAS attempts); no error type
  - concurrency: permit acquisition uses an atomic CAS loop; release increments the count with Release ordering and notifies one additional listener; no FIFO permit reservation guarantee is established
- Usage:
  1. static SEM: Semaphore = Semaphore::new(n); let _guard = SEM.acquire_guard();
- Do not use it when:
  - not for IRQ or other non-sleeping contexts
  - not interruptible by signals: acquire has no error path
  - use kcompletion::Completion for one-shot done/wait handshakes instead of a semaphore initialised to 0

### task_predicate_wait_queue_noalloc

**Allocation-free predicate broadcast wait queue (kcompletion::WaitQueue)** — crate `kcompletion` (`sync/kcompletion`); family `sync.wait_queue`; card [cards/task_predicate_wait_queue_noalloc.yaml](cards/task_predicate_wait_queue_noalloc.yaml)

Wait queue of pinned stack waiters with no stored tokens. wait_until enrols the waiter before evaluating the caller's predicate on every iteration, so wakes between check and park are not lost; notify_all wakes every registered waiter. ktask wraps it as CompletionWait::wait_until.

- Entry points: [`kcompletion::WaitQueue`](../../sync/kcompletion/src/completion.rs), [`kcompletion::WaitQueue::new`](../../sync/kcompletion/src/completion.rs)
- Operations: `wait_until` (each iteration unregisters, re-enrols, evaluates ready, parks if false); `notify_all` (removes and notifies all registered waiters)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: registration is allocation-free (stack nodes)
  - blocking: parks via host closure; predicate must not sleep or recursively wait
  - IRQ / NMI: notify_all is documented IRQ-safe and allocation-free; waiting requires sleepable task context; NMI not stated
  - ownership: unsafe wait_until: caller keeps stack, queue and wake storage alive until registration cleanup, including nonunwinding task exit
  - errors / bounds: no error return from the core; ktask::CompletionWait::prepare returns KError::InvalidInput outside sleepable context
  - concurrency: callbacks run under the queue lock; predicate runs outside the lock and rechecks after spurious wakes
- Usage:
  1. publish the predicate change first, then notify_all after releasing conflicting locks
  2. wait through ktask::completion::CompletionWait::prepare() then .wait_until(&queue, ready) in sleepable context
- Do not use it when:
  - broadcast only (no wake-one); use ktask::WaitQueue when you need notify_one or timeouts
  - no timeout or signal handling

### task_wait_queue

**Task wait queue with condition and timeout waits (ktask::WaitQueue)** — crate `ktask` (`task/ktask`); family `sync.wait_queue`; card [cards/task_wait_queue.yaml](cards/task_wait_queue.yaml)

Linux wait_queue-style sleeping queue built on event_listener::Event and ktask::future::block_on. wait_until / wait_timeout_until register a listener, then recheck the condition before sleeping, so a notify between the first check and registration is not lost. notify_* wake sleepers and can optionally yield.

- Entry points: [`ktask::WaitQueue`](../../task/ktask/src/wait_queue.rs), [`ktask::WaitQueue::new`](../../task/ktask/src/wait_queue.rs)
- Operations: `wait_until` (loop { check condition; register listener; recheck condition; await listener } under block_on); `wait_timeout_until` (as wait_until with a monotonic deadline; returns true if the deadline passed); `notify` (wakes up to N waiters (FIFO per event-listener); optional yield of the caller)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: wait* blocks through block_on. notify_* forwards to Event::notify, which can initialize internal storage/invoke a Waker; with resched=true it additionally yields the current task. This is not a blanket IRQ-safe/nonallocating notification API.
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: queue owns only an event_listener::Event; no waiter storage retained after return
  - errors / bounds: wait_timeout / wait_timeout_until return bool (true means timed out); no error type
  - concurrency: lost-wakeup protocol in wait_until: listener registered, then condition rechecked; plain wait() has no condition (a notify before wait() is lost)
- Usage:
  1. producer publishes the state change, then calls notify_one / notify_all
  2. waiter calls wait_until(|| condition) so the condition is rechecked after listener registration
- Do not use it when:
  - wait* needs a sleepable ktask task. For IRQ producers, separately audit notification allocation/Waker behavior and use resched=false; resched=true yields and cannot be used as an IRQ-safe wake.
  - for one-shot done/wait pairs use kcompletion::Completion; for waits that must not allocate with a predicate use kcompletion::WaitQueue
  - for readiness fan-out to async pollers use kpoll::PollSet

### completion_tokens

**Linux-style completion with caller-owned stack waiters (kcompletion::Completion)** — crate `kcompletion` (`sync/kcompletion`); family `sync.completion`; card [cards/completion_tokens.yaml](cards/completion_tokens.yaml)

Completion counter (complete / complete_all / try_wait / reinit) guarded by a SpinNoIrq, with an intrusive FIFO list of pinned stack waiters. Construction and wait registration do not allocate; signalling is non-sleeping and IRQ-safe. The host supplies a SyncWake notifier and a park closure; ktask provides the task-bound wrappers CompletionWait and wait_for_completion.

- Entry points: [`kcompletion::Completion`](../../sync/kcompletion/src/completion.rs), [`kcompletion::Completion::new`](../../sync/kcompletion/src/completion.rs)
- Operations: `complete` (adds one token and notifies the oldest registered waiter); `complete_all` (sticky completion until reinit; wakes all registered waiters); `wait` (under the completion lock, first consume a token/sticky completion if available; otherwise link the pinned stack waiter, release the lock, then park using the same notification latch as SyncWake; repeat after spurious wakes)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: construction and wait registration do not allocate; complete_all_defer_wake clones an existing Arc
  - blocking: waiting parks via the host closure outside the completion lock (no timeout or signal interruption); signalling does not sleep
  - IRQ / NMI: complete / complete_all / queries IRQ-safe (spinlock with IRQs disabled); NMI not stated
  - ownership: waiter nodes live on the waiter's stack; caller must keep the stack, completion and wake storage alive until cleanup (unsafe wait_with); DeferredWake dropped without wake() can strand parked waiters
  - errors / bounds: wait_with returns unit; ktask::wait_for_completion returns KResult (InvalidInput when not sleepable)
  - concurrency: FIFO notification; token acquisition is not reserved for the notified waiter (a concurrent try_wait may take it); notifications run under the completion lock
- Usage:
  1. task side: ktask::wait_for_completion(&c)? in sleepable task context (InvalidInput otherwise, even if already signalled)
  2. producer/IRQ side: c.complete() or c.complete_all() after publishing the state
- Do not use it when:
  - predicate-style waits that carry no tokens belong to task_predicate_wait_queue_noalloc (kcompletion::WaitQueue)
  - no timeout or signal interruption in wait; use ktask::WaitQueue::wait_timeout or ktask::future::timeout for those
  - ksync::Semaphore is the blocking counting alternative when permits must be returned

### event_listener_event

**Eventcount-style Event with FIFO listeners and stack-allocated listeners (event_listener::Event)** — crates.io `event-listener` 5.4.1; family `sync.event`; card [cards/event_listener_event.yaml](cards/event_listener_event.yaml)

event-listener crate (no_std build, default-features off). Event is a lazily heap-initialised eventcount: listen() or the listener!(event => l) macro registers a listener (FIFO order) as a Future, the caller rechecks its condition, then awaits the listener; notify(n) wakes up to n listeners (additional/relaxed strategies available). Registering before rechecking prevents lost wakeups. Blocking wait() exists only with the std feature; kernel code awaits the listener through its own block_on. Used underneath ktask::WaitQueue, ksync semaphore / rwlock and kmutex.

- Entry points: `event_listener::Event`, `event_listener::Event::new`
- Operations: `listen_then_recheck` (register a listener (heap-allocated for listen(), stack slot for the listener! macro), then recheck the condition before awaiting it); `notify` (wake up to n listeners in FIFO order; returns the number notified; notifications with no listeners are lost)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes with default-features off (cfg_attr no_std unless std); the workspace pins default-features = false
  - allocation: Event::new is const and starts with a null inner pointer that is heap-initialized lazily on first use; listen() allocates a pinned heap listener; the listener! macro uses a stack slot to avoid that allocation; on no_std the listener list is a Vec
  - blocking: the blocking Listener::wait / wait_timeout / wait_deadline are compiled only with the std feature (unavailable in the kernel build); listeners are Futures, so waiting means awaiting them from the caller's executor
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: Event owns an Arc-like inner state lazily; listeners keep the inner state alive; a notified listener dropped without being consumed passes the notification to another listener
  - errors / bounds: no error type; notify returns usize count of notified listeners
  - concurrency: Event is Send + Sync for T: Send; FIFO fair listener queue; eventcount design (notify with no listeners is lost, so register before rechecking)
- Usage:
  1. check condition; listen (register); check condition again; await/wait the listener; loop
- Do not use it when:
  - a notification with no registered listener is lost; always register the listener before rechecking the condition
  - no condition predicate inside Event: use ktask::WaitQueue::wait_until (task_wait_queue) for sleeping-with-condition on the kernel scheduler
  - the std-only blocking wait is not available in kernel builds; an executor (e.g. ktask::future::block_on) must drive the listener
  - for one-shot completion tokens use kcompletion; for poll/epoll fan-out use kpoll::PollSet

### rcu_callback_krcu

**Deferred RCU callback with intrusive node (krcu::PreparedCallback, call_rcu style)** — crate `krcu` (`sync/krcu`); family `sync.rcu`; card [cards/rcu_callback_krcu.yaml](cards/rcu_callback_krcu.yaml)

Asynchronous post-grace-period callback. A CallbackNode is embedded in caller-owned storage, adopted by an unsafe PreparedCallback::new, and submitted without allocating; the callback runs later in non-sleepable softirq context after a grace period. drain_callbacks waits for already accepted callbacks (rcu_barrier style). preflight_callback_submission checks admission before a destructive update.

- Entry points: [`krcu::PreparedCallback`](../../sync/krcu/src/callback.rs), [`krcu::PreparedCallback::new`](../../sync/krcu/src/callback.rs)
- Operations: `submit` (consumes the submission right; the node's callback runs after a grace period in softirq context; on rejection the handle is returned unchanged); `drain_callbacks` (waits for callbacks accepted before the call to return (not merely for a grace period)); `preflight_callback_submission` (checks task context and service readiness before a destructive update; transfers no ownership)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: PreparedCallback::new and submit do not allocate (node is embedded in caller storage); drain_callbacks completion waiting does not allocate but its shared drain record Arc follows fatal OOM policy
  - blocking: submit does not wait; the callback and its destruction must not block or unwind (softirq context); drain_callbacks sleeps and needs sleepable task context
  - IRQ / NMI: submit supported from task, hardirq and softirq context after initialization; rejected in NMI; preflight and drain are task-context only
  - ownership: PreparedCallback owns the right to submit one node or release its resources; dropping an unsubmitted handle calls only the cancel function, never the callback; no Clone; node must stay at a stable address until invocation or cancellation
  - errors / bounds: submit returns Err((KError, handle)): InvalidInput in NMI/unwatched, BadState when service unavailable; handle returned for retry; rejection is not permission to reclaim retired data
  - concurrency: accepted callbacks may run before submit returns; callers own serialization and withdrawal; no scheduler or RCU bookkeeping lock may be held at submission
- Usage:
  1. Embed a stable CallbackNode in retained storage with correct layout/provenance recovery for callback and cancellation; withdraw all publication routes, adopt the sole submission right with unsafe PreparedCallback::new, then submit. A zero-offset repr(C) header is one layout strategy, not an API requirement.
  2. teardown: stop producers and reposts first, then drain_callbacks; downstream work needs its own completion protocol
- Do not use it when:
  - callback runs in non-sleepable softirq context: the destructor chain must not block, allocate-and-wait or unwind; for sleepable destruction use Rcu::replace_sync (rcu_owned_krcu) or kfinalize/kworkng deferred drop
  - drain_callbacks waits for accepted callbacks only; it is not a substitute for withdrawing data and waiting for readers (synchronize_rcu)
  - unsafe API with strict storage and provenance obligations; for plain Box replacement prefer krcu::Rcu

### rcu_list_krcu_list

**Append-only forward RCU list with deferred removal (krcu_list::RcuList)** — crate `krcu-list` (`util/krcu-list`); family `sync.rcu`; card [cards/rcu_list_krcu_list.yaml](cards/rcu_list_krcu_list.yaml)

Singly linked list whose readers iterate under a krcu ReadScope without taking the writer lock. Writers append (push_back, serialized by a SpinNoPreempt writer lock) or remove the first matching entry (remove_first), which unlinks it and schedules destruction after a grace period. Iteration is not a snapshot.

- Entry points: [`krcu_list::RcuList`](../../util/krcu-list/src/lib.rs), [`krcu_list::Entry::new`](../../util/krcu-list/src/lib.rs), [`krcu_list::RcuList::new`](../../util/krcu-list/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `push_back` (appends a prepared Entry under the writer lock; no allocation and no grace-period wait); `iter` (forward iterator tied to a ReadScope; allocates nothing, clones nothing); `remove_first` (unlinks the first entry matching a predicate (under the writer lock) and retires it via an RCU callback; returns Ok(false) for no match)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: Entry::new allocates once (Box); push_back, iter and RcuList::new do not allocate
  - blocking: readers never acquire the writer lock; writers serialize under SpinNoPreempt. remove_first requires sleepable watched task context outside read scopes, but preflight is an admission check, not a grace-period wait. Callback destruction must not block.
  - IRQ / NMI: mutation (push_back, remove_first) only from task context, never IRQ/softirq/NMI; readers may use task scopes or watched interrupt/NMI scopes
  - ownership: each published entry owns one allocation; removed entries are owned by their RCU callback; dropping the list frees still-linked entries in the dropping context
  - errors / bounds: remove_first returns KResult&lt;bool>: RCU admission errors are returned before the predicate runs or the list changes; payload must be Send + Sync + 'static
  - concurrency: traversal concurrent with serialized insertion and removal; iterator is not a snapshot (additions and removals may or may not be observed); no tail-removal or index operations
- Usage:
  1. prepare Entry::new(value) outside writer exclusion, push_back in task context, iterate with an existing krcu ReadScope, remove with remove_first from sleepable task context outside read scopes
- Do not use it when:
  - append and remove-first only; no insertion at arbitrary positions, no removal by handle, no bidirectional iteration
  - removed payload (T) release chain must be nonblocking and valid in RCU callback (softirq) context; T must be Send + Sync + 'static
  - mutation is task-context only; not for lists updated from IRQ handlers
  - for a plain index-keyed lock-free-read map use sparse_index_xarray; for a general intrusive list see intrusive_list_* cards
  - remove_first predicate runs under writer exclusion: it must not block, allocate or reenter writers. Post-withdrawal submission rejection is a fatal invariant failure, not a recoverable KResult error.

### rcu_owned_krcu

**RCU-protected owning pointer with scoped reads and synchronous replace (krcu::Rcu)** — crate `krcu` (`sync/krcu`); family `sync.rcu`; card [cards/rcu_owned_krcu.yaml](cards/rcu_owned_krcu.yaml)

Kernel RCU publication container. Rcu&lt;T> owns the currently published Box&lt;T>; readers borrow it inside a read scope (with_read / with_interrupt_read) without locks or reference counts, and replace_sync swaps in a new allocation, waits one grace period and returns the old Box. Several old versions may coexist while their readers finish. Not a lock and not an atomic multi-object snapshot.

- Entry points: [`krcu::Rcu`](../../sync/krcu/src/owned.rs), [`krcu::Rcu::new`](../../sync/krcu/src/owned.rs)
- Operations: `read` (borrow the published value for the duration of a scope; only owned results may escape; the reader never blocks writers); `replace_sync` (atomically exchanges the published allocation, waits for a grace period, returns the old Box (or the unused new Box with an error and no exchange)); `synchronize_rcu` (low-level wait for a future grace period for callers that withdrew and retain their own objects; unsafe)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: Rcu::new takes an existing Box and does not allocate; reads do not allocate; replace_sync preparation and wait do not allocate, but callback storage still uses the kernel's fatal OOM policy
  - blocking: read scopes must not voluntarily sleep or yield (preemption and migration allowed); replace_sync and synchronize_rcu sleep until the grace period ends and need sleepable task context outside read scopes
  - IRQ / NMI: readers: with_read panics in IRQ/NMI/BH-disabled context; with_interrupt_read is the entry for initialized hardirq, softirq and NMI handlers. Waiting (replace_sync) is not allowed there
  - ownership: Rcu&lt;T> owns the current Box&lt;T>; readers get only scoped shared borrows tied to the scope; dropping the container drops the current value directly with no grace period
  - errors / bounds: replace_sync returns Err((KError, unused Box)) with InvalidInput outside sleepable task context (including inside a read scope) or BadState before service readiness; publication unchanged on error
  - concurrency: lock-free readers (Acquire load of an AtomicPtr); concurrent replacements may overlap and each gets its own displaced allocation; not CAS and not a lock for interior mutable state; Sync only for T: Send + Sync
- Usage:
  1. initialize the boot RCU service (init_service) before any wait or read
  2. read inside with_read / Rcu::with_read in task context, or with_interrupt_read in a watched IRQ/NMI handler; do not voluntarily sleep inside
  3. update with replace_sync from sleepable task context holding no lock needed by readers
- Do not use it when:
  - Rcu is not a lock: it does not serialize writers, protect interior-mutable state, or give an atomic snapshot across two containers; use one Rcu for a snapshot replaced atomically
  - replace_sync sleeps for a grace period: not usable from IRQ/softirq/NMI, with IRQs or preemption disabled, or inside a read scope; use PreparedCallback (rcu_callback_krcu) for asynchronous destruction
  - read scopes forbid voluntary sleep; data read in a scope that must sleep needs its own reference (e.g. Arc&lt;T> cloned inside the scope)
  - replace_sync is an exchange, not compare-and-swap: overlapping successful callers each receive the allocation displaced by their own exchange, which may be the original value or an earlier replacement. It does not serialize a read-modify-write transaction.

### once_lazy_klazy

**Spin-based one-time init cell, lazy value and lazy_static! macro (klazy::Once / Lazy / lazy_static)** — crate `klazy` (`util/klazy`); family `sync.once_lazy`; card [cards/once_lazy_klazy.yaml](cards/once_lazy_klazy.yaml)

no_std one-time initialization for statics. Once&lt;T> runs a closure exactly once (call_once, fallible try_call_once that stays retryable, wait/poll that spin until initialized) and hands out &T; Lazy&lt;T, F> wraps it as a deref-initialized value usable in statics; lazy_static! declares `static ref NAME: T = init` statics that deref to T like the lazy_static crate. Coordination during initialization is a spin-wait; there is no sleeping.

- Entry points: [`klazy::Once`](../../util/klazy/src/once.rs), [`klazy::Once::new`](../../util/klazy/src/once.rs), [`klazy::Once::initialized`](../../util/klazy/src/once.rs), [`klazy::Lazy`](../../util/klazy/src/lazy.rs), [`klazy::Lazy::new`](../../util/klazy/src/lazy.rs)
- Operations: `call_once` (runs the closure on the first call, stores its value, returns &T; other callers spin-wait during initialization; try_call_once resets to uninitialized on Err so it can be retried); `wait_poll` (get is a non-blocking Option&lt;&T>; poll spins while initializing and returns None if initialization never began; wait spins until a value exists); `lazy_force` (Lazy::new is const (static-friendly); first Deref or force runs the factory once)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: Once and Lazy store the value inline (MaybeUninit&lt;T>) and do not themselves allocate; the init closure may
  - blocking: coordination uses spin-wait without a sleeping wait primitive or timeout; contenders spin while initialization is running. This does not constrain arbitrary work performed by the supplied initializer.
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the cell owns the value for its lifetime and hands out shared references; no way to take the value out of a shared cell; Lazy consumes its factory exactly once
  - errors / bounds: if the init closure panics the cell is permanently poisoned and later accesses panic; try_call_once returns the closure's Err and stays retryable
  - concurrency: Once&lt;T> is Sync for T: Send + Sync; after initialization access is a single atomic load; Lazy&lt;T, F> is Sync when Once&lt;T>: Sync and F: Send
- Usage:
  1. declare `static X: klazy::Once<T> = klazy::Once::new()` or `static X: Lazy<T> = Lazy::new(|| ...)` and access through call_once / Deref
- Do not use it when:
  - initialization spins (no sleep): the init closure must not block, sleep, or wait on this same cell; a task preempted inside the closure makes waiters spin
  - a panicking init closure poisons the cell permanently (Once::call_once); use try_call_once for fallible initialization that can be retried
  - Once/Lazy give only shared references after init; there is no take / reset / get_mut-after-share. For boot-time set-once-then-read globals set explicitly (init_once) use the lazyinit card (once_lazy_lazyinit)
  - IRQ/NMI-safety of the spin-wait is not documented in the crate API; do not assume it is usable from NMI

### once_lazy_lazyinit

**Explicitly initialized static cell (lazyinit::LazyInit)** — crates.io `lazyinit` 0.2.2; family `sync.once_lazy`; card [cards/once_lazy_lazyinit.yaml](cards/once_lazy_lazyinit.yaml)

LazyInit&lt;T> is a const-constructible, spin-based, set-once cell for statics that are filled in later at boot (init_once / call_once), then read through Deref. Dereferencing before initialization panics. Unlike klazy::Lazy the value is supplied by the caller at init time rather than by a stored factory closure.

- Entry points: `lazyinit::LazyInit`, `lazyinit::LazyInit::new`
- Operations: `init_once` (stores a ready value once; panics if already initialized); `call_once` (runs the initializer only for the successful UNINIT->INITIALIZING contender; an already initialized call returns None immediately; a caller observing INITIALIZING spins until it finishes, then returns None); `get` (non-panicking Option&lt;&T> access)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: value stored inline (UnsafeCell&lt;MaybeUninit&lt;T>>); the cell does not allocate
  - blocking: losing racers spin (spin_loop) until the winner finishes; no sleeping
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: cell owns the value; Deref/DerefMut and get/get_mut hand out references; Drop drops the value if initialized
  - errors / bounds: Deref and DerefMut panic when uninitialized; init_once panics on double init; get/get_mut return Option
  - concurrency: Sync for T: Send + Sync; state machine UNINIT/INITIALIZING/INITED on an AtomicU8 with compare_exchange; init closure run by exactly one caller
- Usage:
  1. declare `static X: LazyInit<T> = LazyInit::new();` and call init_once exactly once during boot, then use X through Deref
- Do not use it when:
  - set-once only: no reset or replacement of the value; use klazy::Once for factory-based lazy initialization with poisoning semantics (once_lazy_klazy)
  - Deref before initialization panics; callers must guarantee boot ordering or use get()
  - init spin-wait only; do not initialize from a path that can be preempted for long or interrupted by code needing the same cell
  - call_once has no poison/reset guard around f(): if f unwinds after INITIALIZING is stored, later contenders can spin forever. Do not promise poisoning/retry behavior equivalent to klazy::Once.

### deferred_arc_kfinalize

**Arc-like shared owner whose last drop destroys the payload on a worker (kfinalize::DeferredArc)** — crate `kfinalize` (`util/kfinalize`); family `sync.deferred_drop`; card [cards/deferred_arc_kfinalize.yaml](cards/deferred_arc_kfinalize.yaml)

DeferredArc&lt;T> / DeferredWeak&lt;T> use standard Arc counting and hand final payload destruction to prepared normal-worker carriers. Last strong Drop does not sleep or allocate a carrier, but metadata deallocation and queue notification still impose caller-lock constraints. NMI strong/Weak release requires the kernel provider and initialized local irq_work; unsupported delivery is fatal. Construction prepares three allocations; shared finalization is serial and opt-in for a proven destruction-context mismatch.

- Entry points: [`kfinalize::DeferredArc`](../../util/kfinalize/src/lib.rs), [`kfinalize::DeferredWeak`](../../util/kfinalize/src/lib.rs), [`kfinalize::DeferredArc::new`](../../util/kfinalize/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `new` (prepares identity, payload and carrier allocations; Err returns the error and the unchanged value); `clone_drop` (clone / downgrade / upgrade use standard Arc counting; last strong drop submits the prepared finalization); `into_raw_from_raw` (transfer one strong count to a raw payload pointer (intrusive adapters) and recover it exactly once)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], nightly allocator_api)
  - allocation: construction prepares three allocations per object (identity, payload with raw-owner header, carrier); last-strong Drop transfers a prepared obligation without allocating a carrier; metadata frees inline outside NMI
  - blocking: last strong Drop does not sleep; payload destruction runs on normal sleepable workers; the shared finalizer is serial so a sleeping destructor delays later objects; construction needs sleepable task context
  - IRQ / NMI: final strong release may run in task, softirq or hardirq context; NMI release requires the kernel provider and initialized local irq_work and hands off to ordinary IRQ then worker; construction is never allowed in hardirq, softirq or NMI
  - ownership: shared ownership via standard Arc counts; Weak stops upgrading as soon as the last strong owner is gone, independently of worker progress; dropping an owner is not a completion barrier; no public drain, unwrap or mutable-access API
  - errors / bounds: new returns Err((CreateError, T)) with InvalidContext (not sleepable task) or NotReady (provider not installed); allocation and provider invariant failures follow kernel policy; T must be Send + Sync + 'static
  - concurrency: Send + Sync for T: Send + Sync; counting is Arc's; only the final Drop transfers exclusive destruction to the prepared provider; destructor must not wait on another finalization on the same executor (even indirectly)
- Usage:
  1. construct with DeferredArc::new from sleepable task context after the provider is installed; share with clone; last drop (any supported context) defers payload destruction to a worker
- Do not use it when:
  - not a general Arc replacement or performance optimization: use plain Arc when the full destructor chain is legal wherever the last owner can drop
  - destruction is asynchronous and serial on a shared worker; dropping an owner is not a completion or shutdown barrier and has no latency bound
  - payload destructor must not form a dependency cycle with the shared worker pool or wait for another object's finalization
  - construction requires sleepable task context and an installed provider; not usable before the kworkng services exist (except the audited unsafe boot constructor)
  - T must be Send + Sync + 'static; no Arc::get_mut / unwrap / try_unwrap equivalents

## Tasks, work and timers

### work_delayed_kworkng

**Owned delayed work with prepared timer (kworkng::DelayedWorkHandle)** — crate `kworkng` (`task/kworkng`); family `task.work`; card [cards/work_delayed_kworkng.yaml](cards/work_delayed_kworkng.yaml)

delayed_work equivalent: cloneable owner of one delayed callback whose timer is prepared once. queue / queue_default arm it after a TimeSpan (zero delay queues without waiting for a tick and never runs inline), modify / modify_default re-time it or queue it if idle, flush expedites the captured work, cancel_sync discards, shutdown closes and drains Work plus timer delivery. Callbacks run in normal worker tasks.

- Entry points: [`kworkng::DelayedWorkHandle`](../../task/kworkng/src/delayed_work_handle.rs), [`kworkng::DelayedWorkHandle::new`](../../task/kworkng/src/delayed_work_handle.rs)
- Operations: `queue_modify` (queue_default does not replace pending work; modify_default replaces its delay or queues an occurrence when none is pending; a running callback is not interrupted); `flush` (expedites the captured work and waits; not a wait for the original timer deadline and does not follow later retiming)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: preparation allocates (stable Work, timer and reclamation storage, sleepable context); queue / modify are IRQ-compatible and allocation-free
  - blocking: queue/modify/cancel_pending do not sleep; flush, cancel_sync and shutdown need sleepable task context; callbacks run in normal worker tasks
  - IRQ / NMI: prepared queue/modify valid in task, BH or hard IRQ; NMI unsupported
  - ownership: last handle Drop asynchronously cancels and drains Work and physical timer delivery before destroying captures; shut down each delayed handle before closing a private queue
  - errors / bounds: queue/modify return Result&lt;LogicalCpuId, ArmError> (Admission(Closed) after shutdown, or queue/timer validation errors); flush returns DelayedFlushError; positive delays use monotonic time
  - concurrency: concurrent modification can retire the captured flush obligation without executing it; nonblocking cancellation alone does not prove physical timer delivery has ended
- Do not use it when:
  - callback runs in a worker task after the delay, never in timer/IRQ context; for a raw timer callback in timer context use the ktimer-core card (timer_core_ktimer_core)
  - not a periodic timer: re-arm explicitly (modify / queue) from the callback or elsewhere
  - flush does not wait for the original deadline (it expedites); use cancel_sync to discard
  - prepare only in sleepable task context after kworkng services start

### work_handle_kworkng

**Owned deferred work on per-CPU worker tasks (kworkng::WorkHandle / NormalQueue / queue_static_work)** — crate `kworkng` (`task/kworkng`); family `task.work`; card [cards/work_handle_kworkng.yaml](cards/work_handle_kworkng.yaml)

Linux workqueue-style deferred execution. WorkHandle is a cloneable, safe owner of one prepared callback that runs in a normal (sleepable) worker task; prepare it once in task context, then queue / queue_default it from task, BH or hard IRQ context without allocating or sleeping. flush waits, cancel_pending revokes without waiting, cancel_sync drains, shutdown closes admission permanently. NormalQueue is a private queue (per-CPU allowance, routing policy) with flush and close_and_drain; queue_static_work submits kernel-lifetime Work. A pending occurrence rejects another submission (AlreadyQueued): submission is not an event counter.

- Entry points: [`kworkng::WorkHandle`](../../task/kworkng/src/work_handle.rs), [`kworkng::WorkHandle::new`](../../task/kworkng/src/work_handle.rs), [`kworkng::NormalQueue::new`](../../task/kworkng/src/normal_queue.rs)
- Operations: `queue` (submit the prepared Work to a normal queue (default per-CPU queue or a NormalQueue) without allocation or sleeping; Err(AlreadyQueued) if an occurrence is pending); `flush_cancel_shutdown` (flush waits without canceling or closing; cancel_pending revokes pending work without waiting; cancel_sync cancels and drains but allows later submissions; shutdown permanently closes all clones and drains)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], nightly allocator_api)
  - allocation: preparation (WorkHandle::new, NormalQueue::new) is sleepable task context and may allocate; prepared queue/cancel_pending/modify calls neither allocate nor sleep
  - blocking: queue / cancel_pending do not sleep; flush, cancel_sync, shutdown and close_and_drain need sleepable task context and callback progress; callbacks of owned/static normal work run in worker tasks and may sleep, but must not wait for their own Work
  - IRQ / NMI: submission valid in task, BH and hard IRQ context; NMI submission unsupported
  - ownership: WorkHandle clones share one Work identity and shutdown gate; callbacks own their captures (static / Arc, no borrowed stack captures); last handle Drop asynchronously reclaims and may cancel pending work; NormalQueue Drop does not drain
  - errors / bounds: queue returns Result&lt;LogicalCpuId, SubmitError> (Closed after shutdown, AlreadyQueued, admission/ownership rejection); waits return WaitError; creation returns HandleCreateError for invalid context or unavailable services; per-CPU active allowance is configured by QueueConfig, not a worker count
  - concurrency: multi-producer safe submission; a running callback is not interrupted; callback dependency deadlocks remain caller errors; Last handle Drop is not a barrier
- Usage:
  1. prepare WorkHandle::new in sleepable task context, share clones with producers (IRQ handlers included), flush when the callback must finish, shutdown before dropping the last handle if completion matters
- Do not use it when:
  - a pending occurrence rejects another submission: not an event counter; producers needing counted events must keep their own counter and drain it in the callback
  - owned-handle callbacks run in sleepable worker tasks, never inline and never in BH; for non-sleeping BH callbacks use the borrowed-work path (work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng)
  - prepare in sleepable task context only; not usable before kworkng runtime services (kworkng::runtime::init) are up
  - last handle Drop is not a completion barrier: use flush/shutdown before freeing anything the callback touches
  - time-delayed work is a separate handle (work_delayed_kworkng); for raw timers see timer_core_ktimer_core
  - Normal worker callbacks and BH/softirq callbacks have different sleep/IRQ contracts. Do not recommend an owned normal WorkHandle as a timing/context-equivalent replacement for a tasklet.

### work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng
