**Borrowed prepared Work and bottom-half (non-sleeping) work queues (kworkqueue_ng::Work / kworkng::DefaultQueue)** — crate `kworkqueue_ng` (`task/kworkng/crates/kworkqueue_ng`); family `task.work`; card [cards/work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng.yaml](cards/work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng.yaml)

Lower-level, unsafe-publication layer under the owned handles. A caller-owned, pinned kworkqueue_ng::Work is built inline without preparation allocation; DelayedWork additionally prepares an allocated timer and submitted to DefaultQueue::Normal (sleepable worker), BottomHalf or HighBottomHalf (non-sleeping softirq callbacks). The caller must keep storage and captures alive, stop producers and cancel_sync before freeing. Use it for BH callbacks or intrusive/embedded work; otherwise prefer WorkHandle.

- Entry points: [`kworkqueue_ng::Work`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkqueue_ng/src/lib.rs), [`kworkqueue_ng::DelayedWork`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkqueue_ng/src/work/delayed.rs), [`kworkqueue_ng::QueueConfig::new`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkqueue_ng/src/queue/config.rs)
- Operations: `with_callback` (Work::with_callback binds one callback and captures without allocating, publishing an address or invoking the callback; storage must be stable (pinned) before admission); `cancel_sync` (synchronous cancel and drain required before freeing borrowed storage)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: ordinary Work construction does not allocate. DelayedWork::new prepares one timer allocation plus inline Work; queue/handle creation may allocate. Prepared ordinary submission does not allocate.
  - blocking: submission never sleeps or runs inline; BottomHalf / HighBottomHalf callbacks must not sleep; Normal callbacks run in sleepable worker tasks; flush / cancel_sync need sleepable context
  - IRQ / NMI: queue_work valid in task, BH and hard IRQ context, not NMI
  - ownership: queues borrow the Work object, not its owner: caller retains pinned storage and captures until producers are joined and cancel_sync succeeds; Pin is not ownership; Drop does not wait
  - errors / bounds: DefaultQueue calls return ServiceError: NotReady before kernel init, Admission(SubmitError), Delayed(ArmError)
  - concurrency: per-CPU admission and routing; a pending occurrence rejects another ordinary submission; Work state is protected by SpinNoIrq
- Usage:
  1. pin the Work, publish with an unsafe queue_work on a DefaultQueue (producer holds the safety obligation), later cancel_sync in sleepable context before the storage or captures are released
- Do not use it when:
  - unsafe publication: the caller owns pinning, capture lifetime and the final cancel_sync drain; for ownership-safe usage use WorkHandle (work_handle_kworkng)
  - BH callbacks cannot sleep; sleepable callbacks must go to DefaultQueue::Normal or an owned handle
  - not usable before kernel initialization publishes the default services (ServiceError::NotReady)

### worker_pool_kworkerpool_ng

**Per-CPU bounded worker-task pool and bottom-half executors for pluggable work sources (kworkerpool_ng)** — crate `kworkerpool_ng` (`task/kworkng/crates/kworkerpool_ng`); family `task.work`; card [cards/worker_pool_kworkerpool_ng.yaml](cards/worker_pool_kworkerpool_ng.yaml)

Execution layer under kworkng. NormalServices::start creates, on every boot CPU, a pool of worker tasks (bounded by `limit`, growth by a manager task, idle retirement keeping one baseline worker) that pull claims from a PartitionWorkSource and run AcquiredExecution; BottomHalfServices run bounded passes from kirq's Tasklet / High softirq vectors with a source-inspection budget. These are integration contracts, not business workqueue APIs: use kworkng handles for submitting work.

- Entry points: [`kworkerpool_ng::NormalServices`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkerpool_ng/src/normal/services.rs), [`kworkerpool_ng::NormalServices::start`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkerpool_ng/src/normal/services.rs), [`kworkerpool_ng::BottomHalfServices`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkerpool_ng/src/bottom_half/services.rs), [`kworkerpool_ng::BottomHalfService`](../../task/kworkng/crates/kworkerpool_ng/src/bottom_half.rs)
- Operations: `start_normal` (prepares normal execution on every present boot CPU without publishing it; limit bounds workers per CPU, idle_for is the idle-retirement interval (one baseline worker retained)); `stop` (joins all services in reverse construction order after sources are drained and detached)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: source preparation and service start allocate; notification and inspection reuse that storage; worker growth runs in manager task context
  - blocking: start/stop need sleepable task context; BH passes are non-sleeping softirq execution with a turn budget; normal workers are tasks
  - IRQ / NMI: BH passes run in softirq and reject task, BH-disabled task and hardirq context (BottomHalfRunError::InvalidContext); producers publish demand first then call the prepared notification
  - ownership: NormalServices owns each CPU's runtime; integration retains it until producers stop, sources drain/detach and stop completes; Drop does not block or stop runtimes
  - errors / bounds: start fails on invalid context, bad idle interval, empty boot coverage (after joined rollback) or NoMemory for manager entries; worker count per CPU bounded by limit; no CPU hotplug support
  - concurrency: per-CPU services; lock order dispatch -> workers; the provider must serialize BH passes on the selected CPU and never call run_pass inline from its Waker
- Do not use it when:
  - implementation contracts for integrators, not an API for submitting work: submit through kworkng handles (work_handle_kworkng) or the borrowed path (work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng)
  - requires the PartitionWorkSource abstraction and the ktask/ktimer/kirq runtime; not a generic standalone thread pool
  - no CPU hotplug and no public teardown of the global services

### task_sleep_timeout_ktask

**Async task sleep, deadline wait and timeout combinator (ktask::future::sleep / timeout)** — crate `ktask` (`task/ktask`); family `task.timer`; card [cards/task_sleep_timeout_ktask.yaml](cards/task_sleep_timeout_ktask.yaml)

Task-context timing helpers built on the ktask timer. sleep / sleep_until(MonotonicInstant) wait for a duration or monotonic deadline (also sleep_until_boottime / sleep_until_realtime for other clock domains); each wait owns a prepared timer in a TimerFuture, so dropping a pending wait cancels it. timeout / timeout_at race any future against a deadline and return Err(Elapsed) (maps to KError::TimedOut). They are futures: run them under ktask::future::block_on or from an async syscall.

- Entry points: [`ktask::future::sleep`](../../task/ktask/src/future/time.rs), [`ktask::future::sleep_until`](../../task/ktask/src/future/time.rs), [`ktask::future::timeout`](../../task/ktask/src/future/time.rs)
- Operations: `sleep` (completes after a duration / at a monotonic deadline; a past deadline returns immediately; deadlines beyond the u64-ns horizon stay pending); `timeout` (select_biased between the wrapped future and sleep_until(deadline); Err(Elapsed) when the deadline wins; None duration means no deadline)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: a future deadline prepares one owned timer allocation on the first poll; allocation failure follows the kernel allocator policy
  - blocking: async: they yield to the executor (sleeping task until the timer fires); wake comes from a hard-IRQ timer handler
  - IRQ / NMI: the executor's waker must support hard-IRQ wake; polling is task-context; sleep_until_boottime states poll in task context
  - ownership: the TimerFuture owns its prepared timer; dropping a pending wait synchronously cancels delivery and must not happen from its own wake callback or while blocking the callback's CPU
  - errors / bounds: sleep panics if adding the duration overflows the monotonic representation; timeout returns Err(Elapsed) which converts to KError::TimedOut; boottime/realtime variants return clock registration or timer start errors
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Do not use it when:
  - async only: a spin-delay or busy loop on the monotonic clock is the wrong pattern in task context, but these cannot be used in IRQ/softirq/atomic context
  - do not drop a pending sleep future from its own wake callback or under a lock the timer callback needs
  - for a sleeping wait with a condition use ktask::WaitQueue::wait_timeout_until (task_wait_queue); for raw callback timers use timer_core_ktimer_core

### timer_core_ktimer_core

**Per-CPU one-shot hard-IRQ timer core with owned Timer and cancel_sync (ktimer_core::Timer / TimerSet)** — crate `ktimer-core` (`task/ktimer-core`); family `task.timer`; card [cards/timer_core_ktimer_core.yaml](cards/timer_core_ktimer_core.yaml)

Prepared per-CPU timer trees independent of the scheduler. A static TimerSet&lt;N> holds N per-CPU SpinNoIrq timer trees (hardware arbitration and IRQ dispatch); Timer&lt;H, N> owns stable node+handler storage allocated once, and start_on(cpu, deadline) / start_on_if_future arm a one-shot absolute monotonic deadline without allocating. The handler (TimerHandler, hard-IRQ context) may rearm through TimerControl. try_cancel is non-waiting; cancel_sync and Drop wait for in-flight delivery.

- Entry points: [`ktimer_core::TimerSet`](../../task/ktimer-core/src/set.rs), [`ktimer_core::TimerSet::new`](../../task/ktimer-core/src/set.rs), [`ktimer_core::Timer`](../../task/ktimer-core/src/timer.rs), [`ktimer_core::Timer::new`](../../task/ktimer-core/src/timer.rs)
- Operations: `start_on` (starts or replaces a one-shot absolute monotonic deadline on a chosen CPU; past deadlines are accepted and dispatched later, never inline; start_on_if_future rejects an elapsed deadline without replacing a pending one); `cancel` (try_cancel never waits and returns Inactive / Removed / Running; cancel_sync waits for in-flight delivery and removes a pending successor; Drop calls cancel_sync); `rearm` (from inside the handler install the next one-shot deadline under the owner lock; each setting is one-shot so periodic timers must rearm)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: Timer::new / new_on allocate the node+handler storage once; start, rearm and cancel do not allocate; TimerSet CPU slots never grow
  - blocking: start / try_cancel / rearm never sleep; cancel_sync and Drop wait for in-flight delivery (must not be called from the timer's own callback or while holding a lock the callback needs); handlers must not sleep
  - IRQ / NMI: handlers run in hard IRQ context outside timer locks; per-CPU trees are protected by SpinNoIrq; NMI not stated
  - ownership: Timer owns node and handler in one stable allocation; the shell may move but the allocation cannot; Drop synchronously cancels before releasing; a node belongs to at most one TimerSet; static TimerSet required
  - errors / bounds: start_on returns KResult&lt;(owner CPU, newly_added)>: InvalidInput if the deadline exceeds u64::MAX ns or cpu is outside the set; N must be > 0; deadlines are absolute monotonic ns
  - concurrency: per-CPU spinlocks with owner-CPU routing; callback rearm and external starts serialize under the owner lock and the last successful setting wins; start_on is unsafe: platform glue must pin the CPU and notify the actual owner
- Do not use it when:
  - handler runs in hard IRQ context and must not sleep; for callbacks that need a sleepable task use kworkng::DelayedWorkHandle (work_delayed_kworkng)
  - one-shot absolute deadlines in monotonic time; periodic behaviour needs explicit rearm; wall-clock/POSIX interval semantics belong to ktimer (timer_posix_manager_ktimer)
  - start_on is unsafe and needs platform placement/notification glue; most kernel code should use higher-level sleep/timeout helpers in ktask
  - requires a static TimerSet&lt;N> with N = CPU slot count; not a timer pool

### timer_posix_manager_ktimer

**Process-owned setitimer and POSIX timer state with alarm task (ktimer::ProcessTimerManager)** — crate `ktimer` (`process/ktimer`); family `task.timer`; card [cards/timer_posix_manager_ktimer.yaml](cards/timer_posix_manager_ktimer.yaml)

Process-side timer semantics: three setitimer interval timers (ITIMER_REAL / VIRTUAL / PROF) and POSIX timer_create timers with overrun bookkeeping, per-process in ProcessTimerManager. Wall-clock deadlines across clock domains are queued in one global alarm queue served by an async alarm task (spawn_alarm_task) which calls a registered handler with the owner PID; expirations are returned as TimerDelivery values that kprocess turns into signals. Not a generic kernel timer.

- Entry points: [`ktimer::ProcessTimerManager`](../../process/ktimer/src/manager.rs), [`ktimer::ProcessTimerManager::new`](../../process/ktimer/src/manager.rs)
- Operations: `set_itimer` (sets an interval timer for a type and returns the previous (interval, remaining); ITIMER_REAL is armed in the global alarm queue); `posix_timers` (creates a POSIX timer with an allocated id (wrapping counter probing a BTreeMap, InvalidInput when exhausted) and a clock/notification policy); `alarm_task` (one global task waits for the earliest queued deadline across wall-clock domains and calls the registered owner handler with the PID)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: per-process manager owns its itimers and a BTreeMap of POSIX timers; the alarm queue is global
  - errors / bounds: unsupported clock id or exhausted timer-id space returns EINVAL (InvalidInput)
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Do not use it when:
  - process/signal-level timer semantics only: for a kernel callback timer use ktimer_core (timer_core_ktimer_core); for delayed callbacks in task context use work_delayed_kworkng
  - expirations are reported as TimerDelivery values for kprocess to turn into signals; syscall ABI decoding lives elsewhere

### poll_event_kpoll

**Generation-counted broadcast event over PollSet (kpoll::PollEvent)** — crate `kpoll` (`task/kpoll`); family `task.poll`; card [cards/poll_event_kpoll.yaml](cards/poll_event_kpoll.yaml)

PollEvent pairs an AtomicUsize generation with a PollSet. A waiter records the generation, registers, and rechecks has_changed_since before sleeping, so a notify between the check and the registration is never lost. notify bumps the generation and wakes all waiters; notify_defer_wake returns the PollSet so the wake can happen after an outer lock is released.

- Entry points: [`kpoll::PollEvent`](../../task/kpoll/src/event.rs), [`kpoll::PollEvent::new`](../../task/kpoll/src/event.rs)
- Operations: `notify` (increments the generation (Release) and wakes every registered waiter, returning the diagnostic woken count; the deferred form returns the PollSet to wake after releasing an outer lock); `recheck` (waiters compare the remembered generation after registering to avoid a lost wakeup)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (kpoll is #![no_std])
  - allocation: PollEvent::new allocates through PollSet::new (an Arc); notify does not allocate beyond what PollSet::wake does
  - blocking: the notification machinery does not itself provide a sleeping wait; wake invokes user-provided Wakers outside the source lock, whose callback context/nonblocking behavior must be supplied by the integration. Register may allocate.
  - IRQ / NMI: inherits PollSet's IRQ-safe wake; PollEvent itself documents no context restriction beyond that
  - ownership: event owns its generation and its PollSet; notify_defer_wake returns a clone of the PollSet
  - errors / bounds: register returns Result&lt;(), PollRegisterError>; notify returns the usize woken count (diagnostic only)
  - concurrency: lost-wakeup protection via generation counter (Release increment, Acquire load); all waiters wake and recheck their own predicates (thundering herd)
- Usage:
  1. read generation(), evaluate the predicate, register(context), then if has_changed_since(generation) re-evaluate instead of sleeping
- Do not use it when:
  - all waiters wake on every notify and must re-evaluate their own predicate; not a one-waiter handoff
  - carries no payload or completion token; for done/wait pairs use kcompletion (completion_tokens)
  - A finite usize generation wraps. Equality proves no observed change only if a complete counter wrap cannot occur between sampling and recheck; wake callbacks still require the caller execution-context contract.

### poll_set_kpoll

**IRQ-safe poll wake source with owned one-shot waiter registrations (kpoll::PollSet)** — crate `kpoll` (`task/kpoll`); family `task.poll`; card [cards/poll_set_kpoll.yaml](cards/poll_set_kpoll.yaml)

Readiness notification for poll/epoll/select-style waits. A PollSet is a broadcast source of one-shot waker registrations; each logical wait owns a PollRegistrations and uses a PollContext to register with one or more sources (RAII: timeout, interruption or drop unregisters). wake() detaches all waiters under a SpinNoIrq lock and invokes wakers after releasing it, so it is callable from IRQ context. The Pollable trait is the poll()+register() contract; the caller supplies the readiness predicate and must recheck it after registering.

- Entry points: [`kpoll::PollSet`](../../task/kpoll/src/source.rs), [`kpoll::PollSet::new`](../../task/kpoll/src/source.rs)
- Operations: `wake` (detaches every registered waiter and wakes it after dropping the lock; returns the count; a registration cancelled concurrently may still get one late wake); `register` (stores a cloned Waker and returns a PollRegistration guard that unregisters on drop); `pollable` (implementors report poll() -> IoEvents and register their PollSets via the context; caller rechecks readiness after register)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: register may allocate (the waiter table grows through try_reserve, returning NoMemory); wake path does not allocate; PollSet::new allocates an Arc; PollRegistrations::new does not allocate
  - blocking: the notification machinery does not itself provide a sleeping wait; wake invokes user-provided Wakers outside the source lock, whose callback context/nonblocking behavior must be supplied by the integration. Register may allocate.
  - IRQ / NMI: PollSet is an IRQ-safe broadcast source: wake may be called from IRQ context; NMI usage not stated
  - ownership: each logical wait owns a PollRegistrations; dropping a PollRegistration guard unregisters its waiter; guards hold only a Weak source reference so they cannot keep a device or file alive; wake removes the registrations (one-shot)
  - errors / bounds: PollRegisterError: NoMemory, IdExhausted (non-reusable 64-bit registration id space), InvalidState
  - concurrency: waiter table behind a SpinNoIrq lock; waker clone and invocation happen outside the lock; late wakes are possible so waiters must recheck readiness
- Usage:
  1. keep a PollRegistrations alive across Poll::Pending, register through PollContext, then recheck the readiness predicate to close the check/register race
  2. the producer publishes the state change, then calls PollSet::wake (IRQ context allowed)
- Do not use it when:
  - notification only: no predicate and no blocking wait; the caller recheck loop is mandatory (late wakes, check/register race)
  - wake is broadcast and one-shot: registrations are consumed; a woken waiter must re-register on the next round
  - for sleeping with a condition on ktask use ktask::WaitQueue (task_wait_queue); for one-shot done/wait tokens use kcompletion (completion_tokens); for generation-counted broadcast of state changes use PollEvent (poll_event_kpoll)
  - register can fail with NoMemory/IdExhausted; do not unwrap in IRQ paths

### task_block_on_ktask

**Block the current task on a future, with prepared parking and signal interruption (ktask::future::block_on / PreparedTaskWait / interruptible)** — crate `ktask` (`task/ktask`); family `task.poll`; card [cards/task_block_on_ktask.yaml](cards/task_block_on_ktask.yaml)

The sync-over-async bridge of the kernel. block_on(fut) polls a future on the current task with a task-bound Waker and parks the task (park_task) between polls; interruptible(fut) wraps a future so a signal (interrupt_task) completes it with Err(Interrupted); PreparedTaskWait::prepare allocates one reusable Waker up front so a later park() neither allocates nor registers anything. Wakeups are hints: callers recheck their predicate.

- Entry points: [`ktask::future::block_on`](../../task/ktask/src/future/mod.rs), [`ktask::future::PreparedTaskWait`](../../task/ktask/src/future/mod.rs), [`ktask::future::PreparedTaskWait::prepare`](../../task/ktask/src/future/mod.rs)
- Operations: `block_on` (poll the future with a task waker and park the current task while it is Pending until woken; does not handle interruption by itself); `prepared_wait` (prepare validates a sleepable context and allocates one reusable waker; waker() clones it without allocating; park() parks until a wake hint (may return spuriously)); `interruptible` (polls the wrapped future first and returns its value whenever ready (operation progress beats signal delivery; a pending interrupt stays pending); only after the future reports Pending does a task interrupt (signal) complete the wait with Err(Interrupted), as does a poll registration failure)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: PreparedTaskWait::prepare allocates one reusable waker following the kernel's infallible Arc OOM policy; park() performs no waker allocation; block_on allocation behaviour is not documented
  - blocking: parks (sleeps) the current task; park() asserts a sleepable context and that the preparing task is the caller
  - IRQ / NMI: the Waker may be notified from IRQ context; the parking side must be a sleepable task context (prepare rejects masked IRQs, interrupt-like context, disabled preemption and RCU read sections)
  - ownership: PreparedTaskWait is neither Send nor Sync (task-bound); the waker holds only a weak task reference and may outlive the handle
  - errors / bounds: prepare returns KError::InvalidInput for no task, masked IRQs, interrupt-like context, disabled preemption or an RCU read section; Interrupted converts to KError::Interrupted (signal) or NoMemory / InvalidInput (poll registration failures)
  - concurrency: wake hints, not completion results: spurious returns happen, callers must recheck their own predicate and keep their wake source registered while needed
- Do not use it when:
  - block_on parks the current task: sleepable task context only; not for IRQ/softirq or while holding spinlocks
  - block_on alone does not observe signals; wrap with interruptible() for signal-interruptible syscalls
  - wakeups are hints: a hand-rolled park/unpark flag loop must still recheck the condition; for condition waits prefer ktask::WaitQueue::wait_until
  - use PreparedTaskWait when the wake source must be registered before parking without allocation in the park path

## Interrupt deferral

### irq_work_kirq

**One-shot NMI-safe handoff to ordinary hardirq (kirq::irq_work::IrqWork)** — crate `kirq` (`arch/kirq`); family `irq.deferred`; card [cards/irq_work_kirq.yaml](cards/irq_work_kirq.yaml)

irq_work for NMI contexts. A prepared, stable-address IrqWork node is submitted at most once with the unsafe queue(); NMI submission uses atomics plus a certified notification callback; other contexts mask IRQs and pin execution, and the callback later runs in ordinary hardirq context with local IRQs disabled, from handle_irq (bounded by CALLBACK_BUDGET = 64 per invocation). Local CPU only: there is no cancellation, flush, remote submission or CPU-offline protocol. Used by kfinalize/kworkng to hand NMI-time frees to a worker.

- Entry points: [`kirq::irq_work::IrqWork`](../../arch/kirq/src/irq_work.rs), [`kirq::irq_work::IrqWork::new`](../../arch/kirq/src/irq_work.rs)
- Operations: `queue` (transfers a prepared one-shot node to this CPU's ordinary-IRQ consumer; callable from task, softirq, hardirq and NMI after init_current_cpu; NotReady / AlreadyQueued errors leave the node unclaimed)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (kirq is cfg_attr no_std unless test)
  - allocation: allocation-free: nodes are prepared before submission and embedded in caller storage
  - blocking: callbacks cannot sleep and must never wait for work on this CPU; queue is not wait-free (CAS may retry) and has no latency bound
  - IRQ / NMI: submission from task, softirq, hardirq and NMI; callback runs in ordinary hardirq context with local IRQs disabled; handle_irq must only be wired to an ordinary-priority interrupt
  - ownership: no ownership is hidden in the node; a successful submission transfers callback responsibility; the node is one-shot and cannot be reused after execution; storage must stay live at a stable address through callback handoff
  - errors / bounds: QueueError::NotReady (no initialized NMI-safe notification provider on this CPU) or AlreadyQueued; at most CALLBACK_BUDGET = 64 callbacks per ordinary interrupt invocation; no FIFO ordering promised
  - concurrency: per-CPU lock-free incoming list with a claimed flag serializing producers; local consumer only; no remote submission
- Do not use it when:
  - local CPU only; no cross-CPU submission (use kipi call-function or fixed notifications)
  - one-shot node: cannot be resubmitted after it ran; no cancel or flush
  - callback runs in hardirq context with IRQs off and must not sleep: use it only to hand off to a normal worker (kworkng) for sleepable work
  - AlreadyQueued does not return ownership of an existing submission or extend its lifetime; every duplicate submitter needs independent external lifetime protection.

### softirq_kirq

**Fixed-vector per-CPU softirq (kirq::softirq open_softirq / raise_softirq)** — crate `kirq` (`arch/kirq`); family `irq.deferred`; card [cards/softirq_kirq.yaml](cards/softirq_kirq.yaml)

Linux-style softirq/bottom half. Ten fixed SoftirqVec vectors (High, Timer, NetTx, NetRx, Block, IrqPoll, Tasklet, Sched, Hrtimer, Rcu); a handler (fn()) is registered once per vector at init with open_softirq(s); raise_softirq / raise_softirq_irqoff set a per-CPU pending bit; actions run at IRQ exit, BH-enable or in the ksoftirqd daemon with preemption disabled and local IRQs enabled. Actions must not sleep. The Tasklet and High vectors host kworkng bottom-half work.

- Entry points: [`kirq::softirq::SoftirqVec`](../../arch/kirq/src/bottom_half/softirq.rs), [`kirq::softirq::open_softirq`](../../arch/kirq/src/bottom_half/softirq.rs), [`kirq::softirq::open_softirqs`](../../arch/kirq/src/bottom_half/softirq.rs)
- Operations: `register` (installs a fixed action for a vector at init time; returns false if the vector is already occupied; no runtime unregistration); `raise` (sets the current CPU's pending bit for the vector; wakes ksoftirqd when raised from task context on an empty pending mask; the _irqoff form requires IRQs already disabled)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: fixed table of ten optional fn pointers behind a SpinNoIrq plus a per-CPU atomic pending word; actions must not allocate on the hot path
  - blocking: actions must not sleep or depend on process context; raise_softirq does not block (may wake ksoftirqd)
  - IRQ / NMI: raise_softirq usable from task and hardirq context (pins the CPU and masks IRQs); actions run at IRQ tail / BH enable / ksoftirqd with preemption disabled and IRQs enabled; NMI not stated
  - ownership: actions are plain fn() pointers registered for the kernel lifetime; pending state is per CPU
  - errors / bounds: open_softirq(s) return false without changes when a vector is occupied or a group repeats a vector; ten fixed vectors (SoftirqVec::COUNT); restart limit 10 per run (SOFTIRQ_MAX_RESTART) leaves remaining work Deferred
  - concurrency: per-CPU pending word in a cpu_slot; the action table is guarded by SpinNoIrq; raising only touches the local CPU (cross-CPU kicks go through kipi notify_bottom_half / notify_rcu)
- Usage:
  1. open_softirq(vec, action) once during init, publish demand to your own source, then raise_softirq(vec) (from IRQ or task context); the action drains the source
- Do not use it when:
  - fixed ten vectors and init-time registration only: not a dynamic tasklet allocator; per-source dynamic callbacks belong to kworkng BH queues (work_prepared_kworkqueue_ng)
  - actions must not sleep; sleepable deferred work goes to kworkng worker tasks (work_handle_kworkng)
  - raise_softirq only marks the local CPU; to kick another CPU use kipi::notify_bottom_half (ipi_fixed_notification_kipi)
  - NMI-to-IRQ deferral is a separate facility (irq_work_kirq)

## CPU-local data and cross-CPU calls

### percpu_dynamic_kcpu_slot

**Dynamically initialized per-CPU objects from caller-owned memory (kcpu_slot::CpuSlotChunk / DynamicCpuSlot)** — crate `kcpu_slot` (`arch/kcpu_slot`); family `cpu.percpu`; card [cards/percpu_dynamic_kcpu_slot.yaml](cards/percpu_dynamic_kcpu_slot.yaml)

Per-CPU storage for values that cannot be bitwise template-copied (owning, droppable or self-referential types). A CpuSlotChunk is carved from caller-owned backing memory (cpu_count * area_stride bytes); alloc runs an initializer once per CPU with that CPU's id and returns a DynamicCpuSlot handle. get(guard) reads the current CPU's value under a CpuLocalGuard; get_remote needs T: Sync. Dropping the handle drops every CPU's value.

- Entry points: [`kcpu_slot::CpuSlotChunk`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/dynamic.rs), [`kcpu_slot::CpuSlotChunk::from_raw_parts`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/dynamic.rs), [`kcpu_slot::DynamicCpuSlot`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/dynamic.rs)
- Operations: `alloc` (reserves one slot per CPU in the chunk and runs init(cpu_id) for every CPU; on a failed initializer the values already created are dropped but the reservation is not reclaimed); `get` (shared access to the pinned CPU's value under a CpuLocalGuard, or to a remote CPU's value when T is Sync; None for a CPU outside the chunk)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: slot reservation carves caller-owned backing memory with a non-concurrent bump cursor and never reclaims reservations; the user initializer and payload destructor have separate allocation/context behavior.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: safe accessor requires a CpuLocalGuard (excludes local IRQ reentry); NMI not discussed
  - ownership: the handle owns every CPU's value and drops them all in Drop; the chunk must outlive handles (borrowed); initializer failure leaves the reservation consumed
  - errors / bounds: alloc returns SlotInitError: NoSpace (chunk exhausted), Misaligned (backing or stride not area-aligned), Init(E) (initializer failed)
  - concurrency: a chunk is not Sync (allocation is single-threaded); handles are Send + Sync for T: Send; each thread observes only its own CPU's value; get_remote additionally requires T: Sync and the caller must prevent racing access
- Do not use it when:
  - caller must provide the backing memory chunk (cpu_count * area_stride, area-aligned); no allocator integration
  - reservation is never reclaimed, even after the handle is dropped or the initializer fails: size the arena accordingly
  - no mutable access without the unsafe get_mut_unchecked; use interior mutability or a lock inside T
  - for bitwise-copyable boot-time data use the static slots (percpu_static_kcpu_slot)

### percpu_static_kcpu_slot

**Static per-CPU variables via linker templates (kcpu_slot cpu_slot! / CpuSlot / CpuSlotCell)** — crate `kcpu_slot` (`arch/kcpu_slot`); family `cpu.percpu`; card [cards/percpu_static_kcpu_slot.yaml](cards/percpu_static_kcpu_slot.yaml)

Typed per-CPU storage. cpu_slot! / cpu_slot_cell! declare a bitwise-copyable template in the `.cpu_slot.template` section; boot code (begin_cpu_init) copies one area per CPU and installs the architecture per-CPU base register, so hot-path access is base + offset with no lock. Access is gated by capability guards: CpuLocalGuard (no migration and no local IRQ reentry) for any value, or T: Sync for shared atomics; remote CPUs are read only through a published CpuArea.

- Entry points: [`kcpu_slot::CpuSlot`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/static_slot.rs), [`kcpu_slot::CpuSlotCell`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/static_slot.rs), [`kcpu_slot::cpu_slot`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/macros.rs), [`kcpu_slot::cpu_slot_cell`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/macros.rs), [`kcpu_slot::cpu_slot_cell_with_template`](../../arch/kcpu_slot/src/macros.rs)
- Operations: `local_access` (access the current CPU's value under a CpuLocalGuard (any StaticSlotValue), in a short IRQ-masked closure (T: Sync), or without a guard for T: Sync (atomics)); `remote_read` (shared read of another CPU's value through a checked, published CpuArea (T: Sync); no unconditional remote write API); `boot` (copies the template into a CPU's area and installs the base register; BootCpuToken::publish makes the area visible to remote readers)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std], uses alloc)
  - allocation: static slots live in the linker-reserved per-CPU areas and need no allocation at access time; the templates themselves are static
  - blocking: direct slot lookup is address computation; with_current_irq_disabled requires a callback that does not block, schedule, change the CPU base or enable IRQs. It does not establish that arbitrary payload operations never block.
  - IRQ / NMI: CpuLocalGuard excludes local IRQ reentry; with_current_irq_disabled does not exclude NMI (T: Sync required); T: Sync values may be shared with IRQ/NMI contexts
  - ownership: values are bitwise copies of the template, never dropped; types with ownership, drop or self-reference must use DynamicCpuSlot; slots live as long as the kernel
  - errors / bounds: begin_cpu_init returns Result&lt;BootCpuToken, CpuInitError>; unsupported architectures fail to compile; CPU count and area size come from the linker layout
  - concurrency: per-CPU exclusion is established by the caller's guard, not by the slot; CpuSlotCell is Sync only because every accessor is unsafe or requires T: Sync; adjacent CPU areas never share a cache line
- Usage:
  1. declare `cpu_slot_cell! { static NAME: T = init; }` (T: StaticSlotValue), take a kspin::NoPreemptIrqSave (a CpuLocalGuard) and read / write through it; use atomics with current_shared for IRQ-safe counters
- Do not use it when:
  - static templates must be bitwise copyable (StaticSlotValue); Vec, Box, Arc and other owning types need DynamicCpuSlot (percpu_dynamic_kcpu_slot) or a per-CPU array indexed by CPU id behind a lock
  - the guard (CpuLocalGuard, today only kspin::NoPreemptIrqSave) provides exclusion, not the slot: a plain NoPreempt does not stop local IRQ reentry
  - needs boot-time per-CPU area initialization (begin_cpu_init) and the base register; unusable before then and on unsupported architectures
  - remote CPU access is shared-read only for T: Sync; there is no remote write API
  - not a replacement for a plain [AtomicX; NR_CPUS] array when the data must be read cheaply by all CPUs with no area publication or base register (e.g. per-CPU stats scanned remotely)
  - Remote access returns a shared &T for T: Sync; interior-mutability operations such as atomic stores remain possible. It supplies neither exclusive remote mutation nor a snapshot of all CPUs.

### cpu_id_map_kcpu_id_map

**Logical/raw CPU id mapping and NR_CPUS-sized CPU mask (kcpu_id_map)** — crate `kcpu_id_map` (`arch/kcpu_id_map`); family `cpu.mask`; card [cards/cpu_id_map_kcpu_id_map.yaml](cards/cpu_id_map_kcpu_id_map.yaml)

Type-safe CPU numbering. LogicalCpuId (dense zero-based index used for arrays, per-CPU slots and masks) and RawCpuId (hardware id: MPIDR affinity, APIC id, hart id) are distinct newtypes; raw_cpu_id / logical_cpu_id convert through a boot-time table built from the device tree or ACPI MADT (init_boot_cpu_id_map), capped at NR_CPUS. nr_cpus returns the present CPU count (1 before initialization); for_each_present_logical_cpu iterates them. KCpuMask = cpumask::CpuMask&lt;NR_CPUS> with KCpuMaskExt helpers taking and returning LogicalCpuId.

- Entry points: [`kcpu_id_map::LogicalCpuId`](../../arch/kcpu_id_map/src/cpu_id.rs), [`kcpu_id_map::RawCpuId`](../../arch/kcpu_id_map/src/cpu_id.rs), [`kcpu_id_map::KCpuMask`](../../arch/kcpu_id_map/src/cpu_id.rs)
- Operations: `id_conversion` (map a logical CPU id to the hardware id and back via the boot table; None for absent CPUs); `nr_cpus` (runtime present CPU count (clamped to NR_CPUS, 1 before initialization) and iteration over present CPUs); `mask_helpers` (set_logical, get_logical, one_shot_logical and iter_logical on KCpuMask using LogicalCpuId)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: the CPU id table stores a fixed [usize; NR_CPUS] array in a static Once; allocation behavior of firmware enumeration is not established
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: global read-mostly table published once through klazy::Once; LogicalCpuId and RawCpuId are Copy newtypes
  - errors / bounds: conversions return Option (None for absent ids); more CPUs than NR_CPUS in the firmware description are truncated with a warning, not a panic; loading twice panics; AArch64 enumeration requires a device tree
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Do not use it when:
  - ids are stable after boot only: nothing models CPU hotplug
  - NR_CPUS is a compile-time cap (kbuild_config); extra firmware CPUs are ignored
  - mapping is built from the device tree (AArch64/RISC-V/LoongArch) or ACPI MADT (x86_64); not usable before init_boot_cpu_id_map or the runtime lazy load
  - per-CPU data lives in kcpu_slot (percpu_static_kcpu_slot); this crate only provides ids and masks

### cpu_mask_cpumask

**Fixed-size CPU bitmask (cpumask::CpuMask&lt;SIZE>, Linux cpumask_t style)** — crates.io `cpumask` 0.1.0; family `cpu.mask`; card [cards/cpu_mask_cpumask.yaml](cards/cpu_mask_cpumask.yaml)

cpumask crate: CpuMask&lt;SIZE> is a Copy bitset of SIZE bits (SIZE up to 1024, backed by the smallest of u8..u128 or an array of u128) with get/set (set returns the previous value), new/full/ one_shot/mask constructors, first/last/next/prev set and clear index searches, len/is_empty/ is_full, bit operators (& | ^ ! and assign forms) and an iterator over set bits. In x-kernel it is wrapped as kcpu_id_map::KCpuMask = CpuMask&lt;NR_CPUS> (see cpu_id_map_kcpu_id_map).

- Entry points: `cpumask::CpuMask`, `cpumask::CpuMask::new`, `cpumask::CpuMask::full`, `cpumask::CpuMask::one_shot`
- Operations: `get_set` (read or write one bit; set returns the previous value; index range is only debug_assert-ed); `search` (find the first set bit and count set bits)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test)
  - allocation: inline storage only (a primitive integer or [u128; N]), Copy type; no heap
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: CpuMask is a Copy value; get/search/count take it by value, set requires &mut self; iterators borrow the mask.
  - errors / bounds: maximum SIZE 1024; one_shot and from_raw_bits panic on an out-of-range value; get/set/mask only debug_assert the range, so out-of-range indices are not reliably rejected in release builds
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Do not use it when:
  - plain value type (no atomics in its API): concurrent updates (e.g. an online mask touched from several CPUs) need an external atomic or lock
  - SIZE is a const generic bounded by 1024; kernel code should use the NR_CPUS-sized alias kcpu_id_map::KCpuMask with LogicalCpuId helpers instead of raw usize indices (cpu_id_map_kcpu_id_map)
  - hand-rolled `1 << cpu` masks in u64/usize cannot represent more than 64 CPUs; use this type when NR_CPUS can exceed 64

### ipi_call_function_kipi

**Run a closure on another CPU via IPI (kipi::run_on_cpu / run_on_each_cpu, smp_call_function)** — crate `kipi` (`arch/kipi`); family `cpu.ipi`; card [cards/ipi_call_function_kipi.yaml](cards/ipi_call_function_kipi.yaml)

Cross-CPU function call. Each CPU owns an IPI event queue (a SpinNoIrq VecDeque stored in a per-CPU slot); run_on_cpu(dest, closure) runs the closure synchronously when dest is the current CPU, otherwise pushes it to the destination queue and raises the shared IPI, so it later runs from that CPU's IPI handler. run_on_each_cpu runs locally at once and queues for all others; run_on_each_cpu_via_ipi makes every CPU, including the caller, run it from IPI context. The call is asynchronous: there is no wait-for-completion.

- Entry points: [`kipi::run_on_cpu`](../../arch/kipi/src/lib.rs), [`kipi::init`](../../arch/kipi/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `run_on_cpu` (runs the callback inline on the current CPU, otherwise enqueues it on the destination CPU's queue and sends the IPI; the prepared form takes a pre-allocated Callback owner); `broadcast` (run_on_each_cpu runs on the caller immediately and queues for all other CPUs; the _via_ipi form also queues the caller's own copy so all run in IPI context)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std unless test, uses alloc)
  - allocation: remote run_on_cpu allocates a callback owner with NOWAIT before taking the queue lock (NoMemory on failure, captures dropped in caller context); queue VecDeque growth is infallible; run_on_each_cpu shares an Arc without per-target allocation
  - blocking: the call itself does not wait for execution; remotely executed callback bodies and capture destruction must not sleep, acquire IPI queue locks or wait for queued callbacks
  - IRQ / NMI: sending permitted from task or IRQ context, not NMI and not an allocator-reentrant path; remote callbacks run in the IPI interrupt handler
  - ownership: closure must be FnOnce + Send + 'static; the callback owner is queued and consumed on the target CPU; on validation failure it is dropped in the caller's context without invocation
  - errors / bounds: KipiError: InvalidCpuId (outside NR_CPUS or not present), TargetCpuNotReady (destination queue not initialized), NoMemory, QueueFull, CallbackFailed
  - concurrency: per-CPU FIFO queues serialized by SpinNoIrq; callbacks from one queue run in enqueue order; IPI readiness is published with Release/Acquire per CPU
- Usage:
  1. every CPU must call kipi::init() after its CPU slot area is published, before it can receive callbacks
- Do not use it when:
  - No completion barrier is supplied. Use a separately audited completion protocol from sleepable context if needed; never wait while holding resources required by target callbacks. Translation flushes use kipi::tlb.
  - callbacks run in IPI interrupt context on remote CPUs: no sleeping, no taking IPI queue locks; sending is forbidden from NMI
  - requires kipi::init() on the target CPU (TargetCpuNotReady otherwise); the smp feature compiles the SMP-only parts
  - for allocation-free fixed requests (reschedule, BH kick, RCU kick) use the pending-flag transport (ipi_fixed_notification_kipi) instead of queueing a closure

### ipi_fixed_notification_kipi

**Allocation-free fixed-reason CPU kicks over IPI (kipi::notify_reschedule / notify_bottom_half / notify_rcu)** — crate `kipi` (`arch/kipi`); family `cpu.ipi`; card [cards/ipi_fixed_notification_kipi.yaml](cards/ipi_fixed_notification_kipi.yaml)

Fixed set of cross-CPU requests carried as bits in a per-CPU atomic pending word (RESCHEDULE, TIMER_REPROGRAM, BOTTOM_HALF, HIGHPRI_BOTTOM_HALF, RCU) plus one shared IPI. A sender sets the bit with one fetch_or and sends the IPI; the receiver's handler takes the bits and calls the scheduler, timer, or raises the matching softirq. Requests coalesce, nothing is allocated or queued, it may be used with IRQs disabled and scheduler locks held, and requests made before enable_fixed_notifications are retained for a boot drain. It carries no closure.

- Entry points: [`kipi::enable_fixed_notifications`](../../arch/kipi/src/notification.rs)
- Operations: `notify` (sets the reason bit in the destination CPU's pending word (one fetch_or) and, once notifications are enabled, sends the IPI (also to self); success means accepted, not executed)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (kipi is cfg_attr no_std unless test)
  - allocation: allocation-free; no closure is queued
  - blocking: never sleeps; may be called with IRQs disabled and scheduler locks held (notify_reschedule); callers must release timer locks before notify_timer_reprogram
  - IRQ / NMI: bottom-half kicks may run in task, softirq or hardirq context including with IRQs disabled; NMI and CPU hotplug unsupported
  - ownership: no ownership transfer: only a reason bit is set; the receiving side owns the demand state (source demand must be published before the kick)
  - errors / bounds: Result&lt;(), KipiError>: InvalidCpuId for an out-of-range or absent CPU; fixed five reasons only
  - concurrency: requests coalesce in a per-CPU AtomicUsize pending word; enable and take use the same word so that either the boot drain sees a request or the sender issues an IPI
- Do not use it when:
  - only the five fixed reasons; arbitrary work needs ipi_call_function_kipi (closure queue)
  - success means accepted, not executed; repeated requests coalesce, so it is not an event counter
  - the destination must have its service/softirq action installed before demand is published
  - no NMI and no CPU hotplug
  - NMI/IRQ masking and CPU hotplug semantics belong to each request API. The request bits are notifications, not a replacement for a suspend/resume tick-broadcast timer service.

## Memory, user memory and DMA

### mm_alloc_buddy_byte_engine

**Buddy-system byte allocator (alloc-engine BuddyByteAllocator)** — crate `alloc-engine` (`mm/alloc-engine`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_alloc_buddy_byte_engine.yaml](cards/mm_alloc_buddy_byte_engine.yaml)

Byte-granularity ByteAllocator that wraps buddy_system_allocator::Heap&lt;32>. It is one of the three build-time choices for the kalloc heap (feature buddy). Methods take &mut self.

- Entry points: [`alloc_engine::BuddyByteAllocator`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/buddy.rs), [`alloc_engine::BuddyByteAllocator::new`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/buddy.rs)
- Operations: `allocate_deallocate` (delegates to Heap::alloc / dealloc; allocation failure becomes AllocError::NoMemory)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: manages backing regions/pools supplied by the caller; the backing storage remains exclusively reserved to this allocator while managed. No broader allocation/reentrancy guarantee is established here.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the heap takes exclusive use of each region for as long as it manages it
  - errors / bounds: allocate returns AllocError::NoMemory on failure; add_region always returns Ok
  - concurrency: not internally synchronized; methods take &mut self
- Usage:
  1. enable via the `buddy` feature (kalloc/buddy); init_region / add_region hand it exclusive regions
- Do not use it when:
  - for page-granularity allocation use BuddyPageAllocator (mm_alloc_buddy_page_engine), not this
  - requires the `buddy` cargo feature; not thread-safe by itself

### mm_alloc_buddy_page_engine

**Binary-buddy page allocator over caller-provided regions (alloc-engine BuddyPageAllocator)** — crate `alloc-engine` (`mm/alloc-engine`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_alloc_buddy_page_engine.yaml](cards/mm_alloc_buddy_page_engine.yaml)

Page-granularity allocator implementing the PageAllocator trait with the binary buddy algorithm over up to 64 caller-registered regions. Free blocks are tracked with intrusive links and a bitmap kept in the managed storage; it hands out contiguous page runs by count and alignment and can allocate at a requested base address. Methods take &mut self, so a caller needs its own lock.

- Entry points: [`alloc_engine::BuddyPageAllocator`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/buddy_page.rs), [`alloc_engine::BuddyPageAllocator::new`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/buddy_page.rs)
- Operations: `register_memory` (init_region resets and registers the first region; add_region adds another one (errors InvalidInput for a null / unaligned base or size below one page, NoMemory past 64 regions)); `allocate_pages` (allocate contiguous pages by count and power-of-two alignment (allocate_pages) or at a given base (allocate_pages_at); deallocate_pages returns them)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: manages backing regions/pools supplied by the caller; the backing storage remains exclusively reserved to this allocator while managed. No broader allocation/reentrancy guarantee is established here.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the allocator takes exclusive use of each registered region; storage must stay valid until reset and must not overlap live allocations or another allocator
  - errors / bounds: AllocResult errors (InvalidInput, NoMemory, ...); BaseAllocator::init_region panics (expect) when initialization fails; count == 0 is InvalidInput
  - concurrency: not internally synchronized; all mutating methods take &mut self
- Usage:
  1. construct with BuddyPageAllocator::&lt;4096>::new() (const), then init_region / add_region with an exclusively owned, page-aligned region
  2. wrap in a lock when shared; kalloc keeps it in a SpinNoIrq
- Do not use it when:
  - page granularity only; sub-page objects need a byte allocator (SlabByteAllocator, TlsfByteAllocator) or the slab cache
  - not thread-safe by itself; most callers should use kalloc::GlobalAllocator::alloc_pages which adds locking, per-CPU caches and usage accounting
  - at most 64 regions can be registered

### mm_alloc_tlsf_byte_engine

**TLSF byte allocator over caller-provided pools (alloc-engine TlsfByteAllocator)** — crate `alloc-engine` (`mm/alloc-engine`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_alloc_tlsf_byte_engine.yaml](cards/mm_alloc_tlsf_byte_engine.yaml)

Byte-granularity ByteAllocator that wraps rlsf::Tlsf with fixed FLLEN 28 and SLLEN 32 and keeps its own pool/used byte counters. kdma uses it for DMA bounce memory; kalloc can select it as the heap with the tlsf feature.

- Entry points: [`alloc_engine::TlsfByteAllocator`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/tlsf.rs), [`alloc_engine::TlsfByteAllocator::new`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/tlsf.rs)
- Operations: `add_pool` (init_region / add_region insert a raw memory pool as a free block; add_region returns InvalidInput if TLSF rejects it); `allocate_deallocate` (allocate(layout) returns NoMemory on failure and tracks used bytes; deallocate needs the original layout alignment)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: manages backing regions/pools supplied by the caller; the backing storage remains exclusively reserved to this allocator while managed. No broader allocation/reentrancy guarantee is established here.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the allocator takes exclusive use of each pool for as long as TLSF manages it
  - errors / bounds: allocate returns AllocError::NoMemory; init_region unwraps the TLSF insertion (panics on failure); max pool size 32 * 2^28 per the source comment
  - concurrency: not internally synchronized; methods take &mut self
- Usage:
  1. TlsfByteAllocator::new() is const; call init_region with an exclusively owned writable pool
- Do not use it when:
  - requires the `tlsf` cargo feature of alloc-engine
  - not a typed object cache; no per-type slab semantics
  - not thread-safe by itself

### mm_global_allocator_kalloc

**Kernel global allocator with raw page and DMA-page allocation (kalloc GlobalAllocator)** — crate `kalloc` (`mm/kalloc`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_global_allocator_kalloc.yaml](cards/mm_global_allocator_kalloc.yaml)

The kernel's #[global_allocator]: a two-level allocator with a byte allocator (slab, buddy or TLSF, chosen by cargo feature) for small requests over a buddy page allocator. Besides Rust heap allocation it exposes raw contiguous-page allocation with alignment, DMA32-restricted page allocation, per-UsageKind accounting and memory region registration.

- Entry points: [`kalloc::GlobalAllocator`](../../mm/kalloc/src/lib.rs), [`kalloc::global_allocator`](../../mm/kalloc/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `heap_alloc` (sub-threshold requests use the byte allocator; requests over LARGE_ALLOC_THRESHOLD_BYTES go directly to the page allocator); `alloc_pages` (contiguous 4 KiB pages with power-of-two alignment and a UsageKind; 1-4 page requests use a per-CPU page cache); `alloc_dma_pages` (contiguous pages whose physical addresses are below 4 GiB); `register_memory` (give the allocator memory regions (first call bootstraps, later calls extend))
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: workspace policy requires one byte allocator feature; code rejects no selection and chooses slab before buddy before tlsf if several are enabled. This is the global allocator, not an IRQ/reentrancy guarantee.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: dealloc_pages requires base, page count and category to match a live raw allocation with all use ended; ownership is not verified
  - errors / bounds: alloc / alloc_pages return AllocResult (AllocError); init panics when the page allocator or heap cannot be initialised; the GlobalAlloc::alloc path calls handle_alloc_error on OOM
  - concurrency: byte and page allocators each sit behind a SpinNoIrq; per-CPU caches are accessed with NoPreemptIrqSave
- Usage:
  1. platform boot calls global_init / global_add_memory with a mapped, exclusive region
  2. use alloc::boxed::Box / Vec for heap objects; call global_allocator().alloc_pages for raw page runs and release with the same base, count and UsageKind
- Do not use it when:
  - raw alloc_pages / dealloc_pages are an unchecked ownership protocol; prefer the RAII GlobalPage (mm_page_owner_global_page_kalloc) or the reference-counted PageRef (mm_page_hold_pageref_kalloc) when a page needs an owner
  - for a fallible Box allocation use kalloc_types::KBox (mm_fallible_box_kalloc_types), not Box::new
  - DMA with a bus-address contract belongs to kdma: mm_dma_coherent_kdma and mm_dma_streaming_kdma.

### mm_page_hold_pageref_kalloc

**Reference-counted hold on one physical page (kalloc PageRef)** — crate `kalloc` (`mm/kalloc`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_page_hold_pageref_kalloc.yaml](cards/mm_page_hold_pageref_kalloc.yaml)

One owned lifetime hold on a single 4 KiB physical page tracked in the global page metadata table. Clone adds a hold, the final Drop returns the page to the global allocator's inventory. Grants no content access or mapping rights.

- Entry points: [`kalloc::PageRef`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::alloc_page_ref`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::alloc_zeroed_page_ref`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs)
- Operations: `allocate` (allocate one page (optionally zeroed) with a single hold; the UsageKind is charged once until the last hold ends); `add_hold` (increments the hold count; ReferenceOverflow when the limit would be exceeded)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: takes one page from the global page inventory; adds no control block on clone
  - blocking: final release does not sleep
  - IRQ / NMI: final release may run in ordinary or IRQ context, never NMI
  - ownership: each PageRef is one hold; grants no exclusive content access, kernel mapping or PTE authority; holders keep ownership through any translation / device retirement
  - errors / bounds: alloc_page_ref returns NotInitialized, NoMemory or InvalidInput (AllocError); try_clone_ref returns PageMetaError
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. alloc_page_ref(kind)?; share by try_clone_ref; drop each hold; into_raw / from_raw transfer a hold across a raw physical-address boundary
- Do not use it when:
  - one base page only; use GlobalPage for contiguous multi-page RAII ownership without sharing
  - a PageRef does not map the page or grant content access

### mm_page_owner_global_page_kalloc

**RAII owner of contiguous 4 KiB pages (kalloc GlobalPage)** — crate `kalloc` (`mm/kalloc`); family `mm.allocator`; card [cards/mm_page_owner_global_page_kalloc.yaml](cards/mm_page_owner_global_page_kalloc.yaml)

Owns a run of 4 KiB pages allocated from the global allocator and returns them on Drop. Offers zeroed or aligned allocation, fill / zero, byte-slice views and physical-address translation via a caller-supplied closure.

- Entry points: [`kalloc::GlobalPage`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::GlobalPage::alloc`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::GlobalPage::alloc_zero`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::GlobalPage::alloc_contiguous`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs), [`kalloc::GlobalPage::from_raw`](../../mm/kalloc/src/page.rs)
- Operations: `allocate` (allocate one page, one zeroed page, or N contiguous pages with alignment; NoMemory maps to KError::NoMemory, other errors to InvalidInput); `release` (Drop deallocates the pages with UsageKind::Global)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: allocates pages from the kalloc global page allocator
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: exclusive owner of a page run. Unsafe from_raw must receive sole ownership of a compatible live raw allocation with the same count; because Drop deallocates as UsageKind::Global, it is not an adoption API for arbitrary accounting categories.
  - errors / bounds: KResult; NoMemory for exhaustion, InvalidInput otherwise
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. GlobalPage::alloc_zero()? then write through as_slice_mut(); drop to free
- Do not use it when:
  - not reference-counted or shareable; for shared pages with metadata use PageRef (mm_page_hold_pageref_kalloc)
  - always charged to UsageKind::Global

### mm_alloc_slab_byte_engine

**Size-class slab byte allocator (alloc-engine SlabByteAllocator)** — crate `alloc-engine` (`mm/alloc-engine`); family `mm.slab`; card [cards/mm_alloc_slab_byte_engine.yaml](cards/mm_alloc_slab_byte_engine.yaml)

Byte-granularity allocator implementing ByteAllocator with nine fixed slab size classes (8 to 2048 bytes) backed by an internal buddy allocator; allocations above 2048 bytes go straight to the buddy part. It is the default kernel heap algorithm when kalloc is built with the slab feature.

- Entry points: [`alloc_engine::SlabByteAllocator`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/slab.rs), [`alloc_engine::SlabByteAllocator::new`](../../mm/alloc-engine/src/slab.rs)
- Operations: `allocate_deallocate` (allocate(layout) / deallocate(ptr, layout); a failure is reported as AllocError::NoMemory); `size_classes` (nine classes 8..2048)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes
  - allocation: manages backing regions/pools supplied by the caller; the backing storage remains exclusively reserved to this allocator while managed. No broader allocation/reentrancy guarantee is established here.
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: the heap's backing region must remain valid and unused by others for the life of the heap
  - errors / bounds: allocate returns AllocError::NoMemory; init_region panics when the initial region is misaligned or too small
  - concurrency: not internally synchronized; methods take &mut self (kalloc wraps it in SpinNoIrq)
- Usage:
  1. SlabByteAllocator::new() is const; the heap exists only after init_region (methods unwrap the Option)
  2. enable via the `slab` feature (kalloc/slab or kfeat alloc_slab) rather than constructing a second heap
- Do not use it when:
  - not an object cache for one fixed type; there is no constructor / destructor or typed-cache API
  - not thread-safe by itself; use kalloc::GlobalAllocator or add a lock
  - TLSF (TlsfByteAllocator) and buddy (BuddyByteAllocator) are alternatives with different fragmentation characteristics, selected at build time

### mm_address_types_memaddr

**Typed physical / virtual addresses, address ranges and page iterators (memaddr)** — crate `memaddr` (`mm/memaddr`); family `mm.address`; card [cards/mm_address_types_memaddr.yaml](cards/mm_address_types_memaddr.yaml)

Newtype wrappers PhysAddr and VirtAddr over usize, the generic AddrRange&lt;A> half-open range with checked and panicking constructors, overlap / containment tests, and PageIter / DynPageIter that step through an aligned range page by page. Address arithmetic comes from the MemoryAddr / AddrOps traits (checked_add, wrapping_add, offset_from ...).

- Entry points: [`memaddr::def_usize_addr`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/addr.rs), [`memaddr::pa`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/addr.rs), [`memaddr::va`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/addr.rs), [`memaddr::AddrRange`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/range.rs), [`memaddr::AddrRange::try_new`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/range.rs), [`memaddr::AddrRange::try_from_start_size`](../../mm/memaddr/src/units/range.rs)
- Operations: `checked_construct_range` (return None for start > end or an overflowing start + size, instead of panicking); `range_queries` (half-open containment of an address and overlap of two ranges); `iterate_pages` (iterate page-aligned addresses; constructors return None unless the page size is a power of two and both bounds are aligned)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std except under test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: address types are Copy newtypes over usize; holding one confers no ownership or validity of the memory
  - errors / bounds: AddrRange::new and from_start_size panic on start > end / overflow; try_new, try_from_start_size and the page iterator constructors return None instead
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. wrap raw numbers with PhysAddr::from_usize / VirtAddr::from_usize or the pa! / va! macros
  2. build ranges with try_new / try_from_start_size when the bounds are untrusted
- Do not use it when:
  - the types do not validate that an address is mapped, user-accessible or in a particular region; use the user-memory capabilities (osvm, kuaccess) for access checks
  - no VMA or memory-area bookkeeping here; this is only a value type and range arithmetic
  - alignment-only needs are covered by the free functions in the sibling card mm_align_helpers_memaddr

### mm_align_helpers_memaddr

**Power-of-two alignment helpers (align_up / align_down / is_aligned) in memaddr** — crate `memaddr` (`mm/memaddr`); family `mm.address`; card [cards/mm_align_helpers_memaddr.yaml](cards/mm_align_helpers_memaddr.yaml)

const free functions on usize (and default methods on address types) that round down, round up, take the remainder and test alignment against a power-of-two boundary, plus 4 KiB shortcuts and size constants (KB / MB / GB, PAGE_SIZE_4K / 2M / 1G).

- Entry points: [`memaddr::floor_align`](../../mm/memaddr/src/lib.rs), [`memaddr::ceil_align`](../../mm/memaddr/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `align_down` (round addr down to a multiple of align (re-exported name of floor_align)); `align_up` (round addr up; panics if the result would overflow usize); `is_aligned` (test whether addr is a multiple of align)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (cfg_attr: no_std except under test)
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: pure functions on usize values; no ownership
  - errors / bounds: panics when align is zero / not a power of two, and in align_up when the rounded value overflows usize; no Result variant
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. call the const fns with a power-of-two align; a non-power-of-two align panics
- Do not use it when:
  - align must be a power of two; for arbitrary multiples use usize::next_multiple_of instead
  - panics on overflow rather than returning an error, so untrusted addresses near usize::MAX need a checked path (e.g. MemoryAddr::checked_add)

### mm_address_space_memspace

**Process / kernel virtual address space with VMAs (memspace::MmSpace map / unmap / protect / read / write / find_free_area)** — crate `memspace` (`mm/memspace`); family `mm.page_table`; card [cards/mm_address_space_memspace.yaml](cards/mm_address_space_memspace.yaml)

MmSpace (alias AddrSpace) is a virtual address space: a page table plus a VMA set. It maps linear or runtime-backed regions, unmaps, mprotects, finds free areas, reads/writes bytes through the space, handles page faults, clones for fork, and exposes futex backing resolution.

- Entry points: [`memspace::MmSpace`](../../mm/memspace/src/aspace.rs)
- Operations: `map_linear` (add a linear vaddr-to-paddr mapping (paddr 4K aligned) backed by a linear runtime); `unmap` (remove mappings in a range; error if out of the space or unaligned); `protect` (change permissions of a range); `read_write` (copy bytes from/to an address in this space (via the physical pages) into a kernel buffer); `find_free_area` (search from a hint for a free range of a size and alignment within a limit)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: MmSpace owns its VMA set and page table; user spaces are shared as Arc&lt;Mutex&lt;MmSpace>>
  - errors / bounds: KResult errors for out-of-range or unaligned regions
  - concurrency: methods take &mut self / &self; callers serialise through the Mutex around the shared space
- Usage:
  1. Create MmSpace::new_empty_user(base, size) or new_empty_kernel(base, size), then map/unmap/protect. The kernel instance is held in a global SpinNoIrq&lt;MmSpace>; user-space owners provide their own synchronization.
- Do not use it when:
  - not a page-table primitive - for raw PTE operations use page_table::PageTableMut (mm_page_table_pagetable64)
  - not for user pointer access from syscalls - use osvm / kuaccess helpers (mm_user_copy_osvm); MmSpace::read / write go through the space and need the space handle

### mm_iomap_device_memspace

**Map a device MMIO physical range into kernel virtual space with reference counting (memspace::iomap_device / iounmap)** — crate `memspace` (`mm/memspace`); family `mm.page_table`; card [cards/mm_iomap_device_memspace.yaml](cards/mm_iomap_device_memspace.yaml)

iomap_device(paddr, size, name) maps the 4K-aligned span of a device region in the dedicated I/O virtual window and returns the virtual address of paddr; repeated calls reuse and refcount the mapping; iounmap releases it. Also keeps a registry of device regions for diagnostics.

- Entry points: [`memspace::iomap_device`](../../mm/memspace/src/iomap.rs), [`memspace::iounmap`](../../mm/memspace/src/iomap.rs)
- Operations: `map` (map and refcount; InvalidRange for zero size or overflow); `unmap` (drop one reference; teardown at the last reference)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (memspace is #![no_std])
  - allocation: registry is a Vec behind a SpinNoIrq lock
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: reference-counted mapping; pair each iomap_device with iounmap; pinned boot regions are never auto-unmapped
  - errors / bounds: Result&lt;VirtAddr, IoMapError> {InvalidRange, MappingFailed, NoMemory}
  - concurrency: registry guarded by a SpinNoIrq lock
- Usage:
  1. map once at driver init, cache the returned virtual base, and reuse it from fast paths such as IRQ handlers
- Do not use it when:
  - the returned address lives in the dedicated I/O window; use p2v only for RAM, which is in the linear map
  - map once and cache the base (the doc says drivers call it during initialization); do not call per access
  - Manual iomap_device/iounmap pairing is not device-managed automatic teardown (devm_ioremap). The owner must release each reference after all device/CPU uses end.

### mm_page_table_pagetable64

**Multi-arch page table walk / map / unmap / protect with deferred TLB flush (page_table::PageTable64 / PageTableMut)** — crate `page_table` (`mm/page_table`); family `mm.page_table`; card [cards/mm_page_table_pagetable64.yaml](cards/mm_page_table_pagetable64.yaml)

Generic 64-bit radix page table (x86_64, AArch64, RISC-V Sv39/Sv48, LoongArch64) with architecture-independent PagingFlags. PageTable64 offers query (walk), PageTableMut (from modify()) offers map, remap, protect, unmap, map_region / unmap_region / protect_region and conditional replace_if_same for COW commits, batching TLB flushes until finish() or drop.

- Entry points: [`page_table::PageTable64`](../../mm/page_table/src/table64.rs), [`page_table::PageTableMut`](../../mm/page_table/src/table64.rs)
- Operations: `query` (walk the table for a vaddr; Ok((paddr, flags, page_size)) or NotMapped / InvalidAddress); `map` (map one page of 4K/2M/1G; allocates intermediate tables; AlreadyMapped if the leaf is used); `unmap` (clear the leaf entry and return the previous (paddr, flags, size)); `map_region` (map a contiguous range choosing the largest page size (1G, 2M, 4K); no rollback on partial failure); `replace_if_same` (compare-and-replace a leaf PTE against a snapshot (COW commit primitive))
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![cfg_attr(not(test), no_std)])
  - allocation: allocates 4K frames for intermediate tables through PagingHandler::alloc_frame
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: PageTable64 owns the root frame; PageTableMut borrows it exclusively; frames are released through PagingHandler::dealloc_frame, which consumes one storage ownership
  - errors / bounds: PtResult&lt;T> with PtError {NoMemory, NotAligned, NotMapped, AlreadyMapped, MappedToHugePage, InvalidAddress}; address validity checked per call; map_region does not roll back
  - concurrency: mutation requires &mut (exclusive); the type is generic over a PagingHandler and the crate optionally does SMP TLB shootdown via the `smp` feature
- Usage:
  1. let mut m = pt.modify(); m.map(..)?; m.finish() - TLB flushes are deferred until finish() or Drop
- Do not use it when:
  - low-level per-architecture table; for a process address space with VMAs and fault handling use memspace::MmSpace (mm_address_space_memspace), not raw PageTableMut
  - only the leaf/walk logic - frame allocation and phys-to-virt come from the PagingHandler implementation, so an implementation of that trait is required

### mm_user_atomic_word_kuaccess

**Atomic load / compare-exchange on a 32-bit user word with fault-resolving and nofault forms (kuaccess::atomic_*_u32)** — crate `kuaccess` (`core/kuaccess`); family `mm.user_access`; card [cards/mm_user_atomic_word_kuaccess.yaml](cards/mm_user_atomic_word_kuaccess.yaml)

Exception-table-protected atomic operations on a u32 in user memory for futex and robust-list paths: atomic_load_u32, atomic_u32_eq, atomic_cmpxchg_u32, each with a *_nofault variant that never resolves page faults (safe under a non-sleepable lock), plus fault_in_user_writeable for the slow path.

- Entry points: [`kuaccess::atomic_load_u32`](../../core/kuaccess/src/lib.rs), [`kuaccess::atomic_cmpxchg_u32`](../../core/kuaccess/src/lib.rs)
- Operations: `cmpxchg` (Ok((true, old)) when the word equalled old and new was stored; Ok((false, observed)) otherwise); `nofault_variants` (report a missing mapping as NoAccess immediately so the caller can drop its lock, fault the page in, and retry); `fault_in` (one write-fault attempt for a user word without storing; the caller must not hold a non-sleepable lock)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: fault-resolving forms may sleep in the page-fault handler; the *_nofault forms do not resolve faults and are documented as safe under a non-sleepable lock
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: operates on a user address (usize), never forms a reference to user memory
  - errors / bounds: InvalidAddr when addr is not 4-byte aligned; NoAccess when outside user space or the access faults and cannot be resolved; fault_in_user_writeable also returns OutOfMemory
  - concurrency: atomic with respect to other CPUs and user threads on the word (assembly user_atomic_load/cmpxchg); this is the primitive futex and robust-list updates need
- Usage:
  1. under a spin lock use the *_nofault form; on NoAccess drop the lock, call fault_in_user_writeable (or the fault-resolving form) and retry the whole operation
- Do not use it when:
  - only 32-bit words, 4-byte aligned; no u64 or arbitrary-size atomics
  - a plain AtomicU32 reference to a user address is unsound - user memory must go through these helpers
  - for ordinary (non-atomic) copies use osvm::read_vm_mem / write_vm_mem (mm_user_copy_osvm)

### mm_user_copy_osvm

**Fault-checked copy between kernel buffers and user virtual memory (osvm::read_vm_mem / write_vm_mem and typed VirtPtr)** — crate `osvm` (`process/osvm`); family `mm.user_access`; card [cards/mm_user_copy_osvm.yaml](cards/mm_user_copy_osvm.yaml)

Byte-copy helpers that read from and write to a user address supplied by a syscall, returning a MemError (mapped to EFAULT / ENOMEM) instead of dereferencing the pointer. read_vm_mem / write_vm_mem copy typed slices (alignment checked), read_vm_bytes / write_vm_bytes copy raw bytes, and the VirtPtr / VirtMutPtr traits add read_vm() / write_vm() on raw pointers and NonNull. The fault-checked copy itself is supplied through the VirtMemIo provider (implemented by kuaccess).

- Entry points: [`osvm::read_vm_mem`](../../process/osvm/src/lib.rs), [`osvm::write_vm_mem`](../../process/osvm/src/lib.rs), [`osvm::VirtPtr`](../../process/osvm/src/ptrs.rs)
- Operations: `write_to_user` (copy a kernel slice (or one value via write_vm) to a user address; the provider either copies the whole slice or fails); `read_from_user` (copy user memory into an uninitialized kernel buffer; read_vm() returns a value for AnyBitPattern types); `null_means_absent` (check_non_null returns None for a null user pointer so a NULL optional argument is not an EFAULT)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (#![no_std])
  - allocation: `unknown`
  - blocking: may block the calling task - the kuaccess provider resolves page faults in the calling task and file-backed faults can wait for disk I/O
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: no reference into user memory is ever formed; copies are byte copies into or out of a kernel slice borrowed for the call
  - errors / bounds: Err(MemError): InvalidAddr for a misaligned typed pointer, NoAccess when the provider faults or rejects the range, OutOfMemory from the provider; maps to KError::BadAddress / NoMemory; on failure the destination contents are unspecified
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. pass the raw user pointer to the helper; never dereference it in kernel code. Typed variants require p aligned for T, byte variants do not
- Do not use it when:
  - needs a thread with a user address space; the kuaccess provider returns NoAccess when called from a kernel task without one
  - not for copying between kernel buffers - use slice copy_from_slice / copy_within
  - Copies may sleep on page faults; do not call under spinlocks or with IRQs disabled. kuaccess nofault atomics cover only aligned u32 words, not an arbitrary nofault byte-copy replacement.
  - typed variants fail with InvalidAddr on a misaligned pointer; use read_vm_bytes / write_vm_bytes for unaligned data

### mm_user_load_vec_osvm

**Load a counted or zero-terminated array from user memory into a Vec (osvm::load_vec / load_vec_until_null)** — crate `osvm` (`process/osvm`); family `mm.user_access`; card [cards/mm_user_load_vec_osvm.yaml](cards/mm_user_load_vec_osvm.yaml)

> **Needs an owner decision.** Do not suggest it until these are answered:
> - `contract.errors_bounds`: For a Pod element larger than the remaining window (for example [u8; 64]) the per-step element count can be 0, so the scan makes no progress, and a zero-sized element divides by zero. Should the generic scanner be fixed, or its element types restricted?

Heap-allocating helpers that copy count elements, or elements up to the first all-zero element (NUL-terminated strings, argv-like arrays), from a user pointer into a new Vec, with a fixed 128 KiB scan limit for the terminated form.

- Entry points: [`osvm::load_vec`](../../process/osvm/src/heap.rs), [`osvm::load_vec_until_null`](../../process/osvm/src/heap.rs)
- Operations: `load_counted` (copy exactly count elements of an AnyBitPattern type into a Vec); `load_until_null` (scan up to the next 32-byte address boundary per read (not 32 elements), looking for an all-zero element; the generic scan is not total for all Pod types: size_of::&lt;T>() > 32 can yield a zero-element read and no progress)
- Contract:
  - no_std: yes (crate #![no_std]); these helpers exist only under the `alloc` feature (default on)
  - allocation: allocates a Vec (with_capacity(count) up front for load_vec; grows by reserve for the terminated form)
  - blocking: `unknown`
  - IRQ / NMI: `unknown`
  - ownership: returns an owned Vec&lt;T>; no reference into user memory is kept
  - errors / bounds: load_vec reports alignment/provider errors but reserves unchecked count first (caller must bound it). The terminated scanner has a nominal 128 KiB bound, checked after each batch; it is not valid for all Pod types: T=[u8;64] yields n=0 and no progress, and ZSTs can divide by zero. Do not infer guaranteed termination or an exact-read limit from the docstring.
  - concurrency: `unknown`
- Usage:
  1. call with the user pointer and a count (load_vec) or without one (load_vec_until_null); convert bytes to String with String::from_utf8 if text (kuaccess::vm_load_string does this)
- Do not use it when:
  - the terminated scan limit is a fixed 128 KiB (NameTooLong); a syscall needing a smaller per-argument cap (PATH_MAX) must check the returned length itself
  - load_vec trusts count for the up-front reservation, so validate count against a limit before calling (do not pass an unchecked user length)
  - for a UTF-8 string use kuaccess::vm_load_string, which also maps invalid UTF-8 to an error (see mm_user_string_load_kuaccess)
  - Suppress generic load_vec_until_null&lt;T> replacement suggestions until the owner fixes or restricts the scanner. load_vec&lt;T> is a separate counted operation; byte-string use still needs a caller resource bound.

### mm_user_ptr_posix_types

**Typed syscall user pointers with copy-in / copy-out helpers (posix_types::UserPtr / UserConstPtr, UserRead / UserWrite)** — crate `posix-types` (`posix/types`); family `mm.user_access`; card [cards/mm_user_ptr_posix_types.yaml](cards/mm_user_ptr_posix_types.yaml)

UserConstPtr&lt;T> and UserPtr&lt;T> wrap a raw user address by value and provide read_vm, read_uninit, load_vm_vec, load_string / load_string_with_max_len / load_bytes_with_max_len (const) and write_vm / write_vm_slice (mutable) on top of osvm. UserRead / UserWrite are the unsafe marker traits for ABI types that may be copied bit-for-bit, derivable with #[derive(UserRead, UserWrite)].

- Entry points: [`posix_types::ptr::UserPtr`](../../posix/types/src/ptr.rs), [`posix_types::ptr::UserConstPtr`](../../posix/types/src/ptr.rs)
- Operations: `read_value` (copy one ABI value (T: UserRead) from user memory; representation validity only, not an atomic snapshot); `load_vec` (allocate and copy len elements; caller must bound len before the call); `write_value` (copy a UserWrite value or slice to user memory; not transactional, partial effects possible); `load_string_bounded` (NUL-terminated string with a caller-chosen max length (InvalidInput beyond it, IllegalBytes for bad UTF-8); load_bytes_with_max_len preserves non-UTF-8 bytes)
- Contract:
  - no_std: `unknown`
  - allocation: load_vm_vec / load_string* allocate; read_vm / write_vm copy into caller storage
  - blocking: copy helpers may fault or block; use in initialized thread context, not early boot or a hardware IRQ
  - IRQ / NMI: copy helpers must not be used from a hardware IRQ; cast / is_null / check_non_null perform no memory access
